title: Word sets
description: Numbers, counters, days, dates, months, clock time, colours, family, body parts, positions and pronouns: the closed sets you learn whole.

conventions.romaji: kotoba's stored spelling: modified Hepburn, lowercase, no macrons, long vowels as spelled (sou, daijoubu, kirei), wa/o/e particles, っ before ch = t (kotchi). Leading hyphen = attaches to a word.
conventions.register: romaji = casual form, learned first; polite = desu/masu counterpart, or null when there is no register difference.
conventions.freqRank: rank in jiten.moe drama frequency list (CC BY-SA 4.0); freqNote explains tokenizer-split forms. null = no usable rank.
conventions.contrastGroup: items sharing a group name are learned side by side; their examples share a base sentence.

stages.summary: 97 words in 22 chunks: numbers, counting things, counting people, clock time and 7 more.

stages.summary: 79 words in 20 chunks: counters, years and age, days and years around now, parts of the day and 6 more.

blocks.label: Zero to five
blocks.rationale: Lets you count and read out numbers up to five.
blocks.interference: Yon and shi both mean four; say yon.

items.use: The everyday spoken zero; rei is the formal version used in weather, scores and announcements.

example.ja: バッテリーもうゼロだよ。
example.english: My battery's already at zero.

examplePolite.romaji: batterii ga mou zero desu.
examplePolite.ja: バッテリーがもうゼロです。
examplePolite.english: My battery is already at zero.

items.notes: Rei (零) is heard in temperatures like rei do (0 degrees). In phone numbers people say zero or maru.

items.use: For counting, prices, times and maths; one thing is hitotsu and one person is hitori.

example.ja: 一から十まで数えて。
example.english: Count from one to ten.

examplePolite.romaji: ichi kara juu made kazoete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 一から十まで数えてください。
examplePolite.english: Please count from one to ten.

items.notes: Shortens to i- with a doubled sound before many counters: ikko, issai, ippun, ippon.

example.ja: 部屋は二階だよ。
example.english: The room's on the second floor.

examplePolite.romaji: heya wa nikai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 部屋は二階です。
examplePolite.english: The room is on the second floor.

items.notes: Stretched to nii when reading out phone numbers so it isn't missed.

example.ja: 三時に会う？
example.english: Want to meet at three?

examplePolite.romaji: sanji ni aimasen ka.
examplePolite.ja: 三時に会いませんか。
examplePolite.english: Shall we meet at three?

items.notes: Softens the next sound: sanbyaku, sanzen, sanbon, sanbai. Not the name suffix -san.

items.use: The default four; shi appears in shigatsu (April) and when counting ichi, ni, san, shi aloud.

example.ja: 四番のバスに乗って。
example.english: Take the number four bus.

examplePolite.romaji: yonban no basu ni notte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 四番のバスに乗ってください。
examplePolite.english: Please take the number four bus.

items.notes: Shi also sounds like 'death', so it's avoided. Four o'clock is yoji and four people is yonin.

example.ja: 五分で着くよ。
example.english: I'll be there in five minutes.

examplePolite.romaji: gofun de tsukimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 五分で着きます。
examplePolite.english: I'll arrive in five minutes.

items.notes: Stretched to goo when reading out phone numbers.

blocks.label: Six to ten
blocks.rationale: Lets you count to ten and say times and ages.
blocks.interference: Nana and shichi both mean seven, kyuu and ku both nine; shichi sounds like ichi.

example.ja: 六時に起きた。
example.english: I got up at six.

examplePolite.romaji: rokuji ni okimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 六時に起きました。
examplePolite.english: I got up at six.

items.notes: Shortens to rop- before h and p sounds: roppyaku, roppon, roppun.

items.use: The safe default seven; shichi is standard in shichigatsu (July) and common in shichiji (7 o'clock).

example.romaji: nanasai no musume ga iru yo.
example.ja: 七歳の娘がいるよ。
example.english: I've got a seven-year-old daughter.

examplePolite.romaji: nanasai no musume ga imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 七歳の娘がいます。
examplePolite.english: I have a seven-year-old daughter.

items.notes: Shichi is easy to mishear as ichi, which is why people switch to nana.

example.ja: 八時に電話するね。
example.english: I'll call you at eight.

examplePolite.romaji: hachiji ni denwa shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 八時に電話します。
examplePolite.english: I'll call you at eight.

items.notes: Shortens to hap- or has- before many counters: happyaku, hassen, happon, hassai.

items.use: The default nine; 9 o'clock is kuji and September is kugatsu.

example.romaji: shiai wa kyuu tai ichi datta.
example.ja: 試合は九対一だった。
example.english: The game finished nine to one.

examplePolite.romaji: shiai wa kyuu tai ichi deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 試合は九対一でした。
examplePolite.english: The game finished nine to one.

items.notes: Not the same word as kyuu ni (suddenly).

example.ja: 十円足りない。
example.english: I'm ten yen short.

examplePolite.romaji: juu en tarimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 十円足りません。
examplePolite.english: I'm ten yen short.

items.notes: Shortens to jup- or jus- before many counters: juppun, juppon, jussai, jukkai.

blocks.label: Things one to five
blocks.rationale: Lets you count and order things without knowing a counter.
blocks.interference: Hitotsu and futatsu are things; hitori and futari are people.

items.use: Counts things that have no special counter, and is how you order: kore hitotsu.

example.ja: これ、一つちょうだい。
example.english: Give me one of these.

examplePolite.romaji: kore o hitotsu kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: これを一つください。
examplePolite.english: One of these, please.

items.notes: Mou hitotsu means one more. One person is hitori, not hitotsu.

items.use: The count usually comes after the thing: ringo o futatsu.

example.ja: りんご二つ買ってきて。
example.english: Pick up two apples.

examplePolite.romaji: ringo o futatsu katte kite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: りんごを二つ買ってきてください。
examplePolite.english: Please pick up two apples.

items.notes: Futari is two people; futatsu is two things.

example.ja: 三つで十分だよ。
example.english: Three is plenty.

examplePolite.romaji: mittsu de juubun desu.
examplePolite.ja: 三つで十分です。
examplePolite.english: Three is plenty.

items.notes: Hold the small pause: mit-tsu, not mitsu.

example.ja: 椅子、四つある？
example.english: Are there four chairs?

examplePolite.romaji: isu wa yottsu arimasu ka.
examplePolite.ja: 椅子は四つありますか。
examplePolite.english: Are there four chairs?

items.notes: Hold the small pause: yot-tsu. Easy to mix with yattsu (eight).

example.ja: 五つも食べたの？
example.english: You ate five of them?

examplePolite.romaji: itsutsu mo tabeta n desu ka.
examplePolite.ja: 五つも食べたんですか。
examplePolite.english: You ate five of them?

items.notes: No pause here, unlike mittsu and yottsu.

blocks.label: Things six to ten
blocks.rationale: Lets you count things up to ten.
blocks.interference: Muttsu (6) sounds like mittsu (3), and yattsu (8) like yottsu (4).

example.ja: 卵六つ使うよ。
example.english: We're using six eggs.

examplePolite.romaji: tamago o muttsu tsukaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 卵を六つ使います。
examplePolite.english: We'll use six eggs.

items.notes: Easy to mishear as mittsu (three); listen for mu.

example.romaji: nanatsume no eki de oriru yo.
example.ja: 七つ目の駅で降りるよ。
example.english: I get off at the seventh stop.

examplePolite.romaji: nanatsume no eki de orimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 七つ目の駅で降ります。
examplePolite.english: I get off at the seventh station.

items.notes: Add -me for order: hitotsume, futatsume = first, second.

example.ja: ピザ、八つに切って。
example.english: Cut the pizza into eight.

examplePolite.romaji: piza o yattsu ni kitte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ピザを八つに切ってください。
examplePolite.english: Please cut the pizza into eight.

items.notes: Easy to mix with yottsu (four); listen for ya.

example.ja: 九つあったはずだけど。
example.english: There should've been nine.

examplePolite.romaji: kokonotsu atta hazu desu ga.
examplePolite.ja: 九つあったはずですが。
examplePolite.english: There should have been nine.

items.notes: Many adults just say kyuuko, with the counter -ko.

blocks.label: Counting people
blocks.rationale: Lets you say and ask how many people, as at a restaurant door.
blocks.interference: One and two people are hitori and futari, not ichinin and ninin; four is yonin.

items.use: Counts one person, and with de means on your own: hitori de.

example.romaji: kyou wa hitori de iku yo.
example.ja: 今日は一人で行くよ。
example.english: I'm going on my own today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hitori de ikimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は一人で行きます。
examplePolite.english: I'm going alone today.

items.notes: Not ichinin. Hitorikko is an only child; hitorigurashi is living alone.

items.english: two people; the two of them; a couple
items.use: Futari de means just the two of us or them.

example.ja: 二人で飲みに行かない？
example.english: Want to grab a drink, just the two of us?

examplePolite.romaji: futari de nomi ni ikimasen ka.
examplePolite.ja: 二人で飲みに行きませんか。
examplePolite.english: Shall the two of us go for a drink?

items.notes: Not ninin. Often means a couple: futari no jikan = time for the two of them.

items.english: three people (and from three up: number + -nin)
items.use: Regular from three on, except yonin for four.

example.ja: 三人でご飯食べた。
example.english: The three of us ate together.

examplePolite.romaji: sannin de gohan o tabemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 三人でご飯を食べました。
examplePolite.english: The three of us had a meal together.

items.notes: Seven is nananin or shichinin; nine is kyuunin, rarely kunin.

items.use: The one irregular count of people from three up.

example.romaji: uchi wa yonin kazoku da yo.
example.ja: うちは四人家族だよ。
example.english: We're a family of four.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi wa yonin kazoku desu.
examplePolite.ja: うちは四人家族です。
examplePolite.english: We are a family of four.

items.notes: One n only: not yonnin, and never shinin.

items.use: Asks how many people; restaurant staff ask the same thing as nanmei sama desu ka.

example.ja: 今日何人来る？
example.english: How many people are coming today?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nannin kimasu ka.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は何人来ますか。
examplePolite.english: How many people are coming today?

items.notes: The same kanji read nanijin asks someone's nationality.

blocks.label: Telling the hour
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask and tell the time to the half hour, morning or afternoon.
blocks.interference: yoji, shichiji and kuji break the number pattern; nanji (what time) vs nanjikan (how many hours).

items.use: ichiji, niji, sanji, yoji, goji, rokuji, shichiji, hachiji, kuji, juuji, juuichiji, juuniji; 4, 7 and 9 are the traps.

example.romaji: ashita, yoji ni eki de ne.
example.ja: 明日、四時に駅でね。
example.english: Tomorrow, four o'clock at the station.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa yoji ni eki de aimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 明日は四時に駅で会いましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's meet at the station at four tomorrow.

items.notes: Ichiji alone can also mean 'for a while, temporarily': ichiji teishi = pause.

items.use: Nanji ni = at what time; nanji made = until what time.

example.ja: 今日、何時に帰ってくる？
example.english: What time are you coming home today?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nanji ni kaette kimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日は何時に帰ってきますか？
examplePolite.english: What time will you be home today?

items.notes: Nanjikan is a different question: 'how many hours'.

items.use: After -ji for half past (sanji han); after other units for 'and a half' (ichijikan han).

example.ja: 七時半に起こして。
example.english: Wake me up at half past seven.

examplePolite.romaji: shichiji han ni okoshite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 七時半に起こしてください。
examplePolite.english: Please wake me up at half past seven.

items.notes: Half of something is hanbun, not han.

items.use: Goes before the time: gozen juuji = 10 a.m.; gozenchuu = during the morning.

example.romaji: kaigi, gozen juuji kara da yo.
example.ja: 会議、午前十時からだよ。
example.english: The meeting starts at 10 a.m.

examplePolite.romaji: kaigi wa gozen juuji kara desu.
examplePolite.ja: 会議は午前十時からです。
examplePolite.english: The meeting starts at 10 a.m.

items.notes: In casual talk, asa juuji is just as common.

items.use: Goes before the time: gogo sanji = 3 p.m.; on its own it means 'the afternoon'.

example.romaji: gogo sanji goro ni iku ne.
example.ja: 午後三時ごろに行くね。
example.english: I'll come around 3 p.m.

examplePolite.romaji: gogo sanji goro ni ikimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 午後三時ごろに行きます。
examplePolite.english: I'll come around 3 p.m.

items.notes: Evening times are often said with yoru: yoru hachiji = 8 p.m.

blocks.label: Monday to Thursday
blocks.rationale: Lets you name the first four days of the week.
blocks.interference: Getsu in getsuyoubi is the same moon word as -gatsu in month names.

items.use: Add ni for a specific Monday (getsuyoubi ni); add wa for every Monday or as a topic.

example.romaji: mata getsuyoubi kara shigoto da yo.
example.ja: また月曜日から仕事だよ。
example.english: Back to work on Monday.

examplePolite.romaji: mata getsuyoubi kara shigoto desu.
examplePolite.ja: また月曜日から仕事です。
examplePolite.english: It's back to work on Monday.

items.notes: Literally 'moon day'.

example.ja: 火曜日の夜、暇？
example.english: Are you free Tuesday night?

examplePolite.romaji: kayoubi no yoru wa aite imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 火曜日の夜は空いていますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you free on Tuesday night?

items.notes: Literally 'fire day'.

example.ja: 水曜日までに送るね。
example.english: I'll send it by Wednesday.

examplePolite.romaji: suiyoubi made ni okurimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 水曜日までに送ります。
examplePolite.english: I'll send it by Wednesday.

items.notes: Literally 'water day'.

example.romaji: mokuyoubi wa itsumo jimu ni iku.
example.ja: 木曜日はいつもジムに行く。
example.english: I always go to the gym on Thursdays.

examplePolite.romaji: mokuyoubi wa itsumo jimu ni ikimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 木曜日はいつもジムに行きます。
examplePolite.english: I always go to the gym on Thursdays.

items.notes: Literally 'tree day'.

blocks.label: Friday to Sunday
blocks.rationale: Finishes the week and lets you ask which day something is on.
blocks.interference: Nan'youbi asks the weekday; nannichi asks the date.

example.ja: 金曜日、飲みに行かない？
example.english: Want to go for drinks on Friday?

examplePolite.romaji: kin'youbi, nomi ni ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 金曜日、飲みに行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to go for drinks on Friday?

items.notes: Literally 'gold day'.

example.romaji: doyoubi wa osoku made neteru yo.
example.ja: 土曜日は遅くまで寝てるよ。
example.english: I sleep in on Saturdays.

examplePolite.romaji: doyoubi wa osoku made nete imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 土曜日は遅くまで寝ています。
examplePolite.english: I sleep in on Saturdays.

items.notes: Literally 'earth day'.

example.ja: 今度の日曜日、何する？
example.english: What are you doing this Sunday?

examplePolite.romaji: kondo no nichiyoubi wa nani o shimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今度の日曜日は何をしますか？
examplePolite.english: What are you doing this Sunday?

items.notes: Literally 'sun day'.

example.ja: 次の試験って何曜日？
example.english: What day is the next exam?

examplePolite.romaji: tsugi no shiken wa nan'youbi desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 次の試験は何曜日ですか？
examplePolite.english: What day of the week is the next exam?

items.notes: For the date, ask nannichi.

blocks.label: Saying your age
blocks.rationale: Lets you give your age and ask someone else's.
blocks.interference: hassai and jussai shrink; twenty is hatachi, not nijuusai.

items.use: issai, nisai, sansai, yonsai, gosai, rokusai, nanasai, hassai, kyuusai, jussai; twenty is hatachi; how old is nansai.

example.ja: 娘、八歳になったよ。
example.english: My daughter just turned eight.

examplePolite.romaji: musume wa hassai ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 娘は八歳になりました。
examplePolite.english: My daughter has turned eight.

items.notes: Often written 才 in casual writing.

items.use: The plain way to ask an age; with an adult you don't know well, oikutsu desu ka is softer.

example.romaji: inu, ima nansai ni natta no?
example.ja: 犬、今何歳になったの？
example.english: How old is your dog now?

examplePolite.romaji: inu wa ima nansai ni narimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 犬は今何歳になりましたか？
examplePolite.english: How old is your dog now?

items.use: The polite way to ask someone's age, also used warmly with small children.

example.ja: 僕、おいくつ？
example.english: How old are you, little guy?

items.notes: Plain ikutsu asks 'how many', or 'how old' to a child.

items.use: The special word for age twenty; drinking and smoking become legal at hatachi.

example.romaji: osake wa hatachi ni natte kara ne.
example.ja: お酒は二十歳になってからね。
example.english: No alcohol until you're twenty.

examplePolite.romaji: osake wa hatachi ni natte kara desu.
examplePolite.ja: お酒は二十歳になってからです。
examplePolite.english: Alcohol is for those twenty and over.

items.notes: Twenty-one goes back to the pattern: nijuuissai.

blocks.label: Three daily meals
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about breakfast, lunch and dinner.
blocks.interference: Ohiru means both noon and lunch.

example.romaji: kyou asagohan tabete nai n da.
example.ja: 今日朝ご飯食べてないんだ。
example.english: I haven't had breakfast today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa asagohan o tabete inai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は朝ご飯を食べていないんです。
examplePolite.english: I haven't eaten breakfast today.

items.notes: Asameshi is a rougher version, mostly used by men.

example.ja: 昼ご飯何にする？
example.english: What do you want for lunch?

examplePolite.romaji: hirugohan wa nani ni shimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 昼ご飯は何にしますか？
examplePolite.english: What will you have for lunch?

items.notes: Ohiru and ranchi are also common.

example.ja: 今日の晩ご飯何？
example.english: What's for dinner tonight?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no bangohan wa nan desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日の晩ご飯は何ですか？
examplePolite.english: What's for dinner today?

items.notes: Yorugohan is also common, especially among younger speakers.

example.ja: お昼一緒に食べない？
example.english: Want to have lunch together?

examplePolite.romaji: ohiru, issho ni tabemasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: お昼、一緒に食べませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to have lunch together?

items.notes: Ohiruyasumi is the lunch break.

blocks.label: Mum and dad
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk to and about your parents and other people's.
blocks.interference: haha and chichi are your own parents to outsiders; okaasan and otousan are others' parents, or yours to their face.

items.use: For someone else's mother, and for your own mum when talking to her or at home.

example.ja: お母さん、今日のご飯何？
example.english: Mum, what's for dinner today?

examplePolite.romaji: okaasan wa ogenki desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お母さんはお元気ですか？
examplePolite.english: How is your mother?

items.notes: With outsiders in polite talk, call your own mother haha.

items.use: For someone else's father, and for your own dad when talking to him or at home.

example.romaji: otousan, ashita no shiai mi ni kuru?
example.ja: お父さん、明日の試合見に来る？
example.english: Dad, are you coming to my game tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: otousan mo kimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お父さんも来ますか？
examplePolite.english: Is your father coming too?

items.notes: With outsiders in polite talk, call your own father chichi.

items.use: Your own mother when talking to people outside the family; someone else's mother is okaasan.

example.romaji: haha ga kyou kotchi ni kuru n da.
example.ja: 母が今日こっちに来るんだ。
example.english: My mum's coming here today.

examplePolite.romaji: haha wa toukyou ni sunde imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 母は東京に住んでいます。
examplePolite.english: My mother lives in Tokyo.

items.notes: Calling your own mother okaasan to a teacher or boss sounds childish.

items.use: Your own father when talking to people outside the family; someone else's father is otousan.

example.romaji: chichi wa mada shigoto da yo
example.ja: 父はまだ仕事だよ
example.english: My dad's still at work.

examplePolite.romaji: chichi wa ginkou de hataraite imasu
examplePolite.ja: 父は銀行で働いています
examplePolite.english: My father works at a bank.

items.notes: Calling your own father otousan to a teacher or boss sounds childish.

blocks.label: Family and parents
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about your family and parents as a group.
blocks.interference: ryoushin is your own parents; goryoushin is someone else's.

items.use: Your own family or families in general; someone else's family is gokazoku.

example.ja: 週末は家族と過ごす
example.english: I'm spending the weekend with my family.

examplePolite.romaji: kazoku wa yonin desu
examplePolite.ja: 家族は四人です
examplePolite.english: There are four of us in my family.

items.use: One or both parents, often parents in general; someone else's parents are oyagosan.

example.ja: やばい、親にバレた
example.english: Oh no, my parents found out.

examplePolite.romaji: oya ni soudan shimashita
examplePolite.ja: 親に相談しました
examplePolite.english: I talked it over with my parents.

items.use: Both your parents; someone else's are goryoushin.

example.ja: 両親に電話しなきゃ
example.english: I need to call my parents.

examplePolite.romaji: ryoushin wa oosaka ni sunde imasu
examplePolite.ja: 両親は大阪に住んでいます
examplePolite.english: My parents live in Osaka.

items.use: Someone else's parents; the polite form of ryoushin.

example.romaji: kanojo no goryoushin ni au n da
example.ja: 彼女のご両親に会うんだ
example.english: I'm meeting my girlfriend's parents.

examplePolite.romaji: goryoushin wa ogenki desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ご両親はお元気ですか？
examplePolite.english: How are your parents?

blocks.label: Older brother and sister
blocks.rationale: Lets you mention your older siblings and ask about someone else's.
blocks.interference: ani and ane are your own; oniisan and oneesan are others', or yours to their face.

items.use: Your own older brother when talking to others; someone else's is oniisan.

example.romaji: ani wa ima amerika ni iru
example.ja: 兄は今アメリカにいる
example.english: My big brother's in America now.

examplePolite.romaji: ani ga hitori imasu
examplePolite.ja: 兄が一人います
examplePolite.english: I have one older brother.

items.notes: To his face you say oniichan or his name, never ani.

items.use: Someone else's older brother, or what you call your own to his face.

example.ja: お兄さんは今何歳？
example.english: How old is your brother now?

examplePolite.romaji: oniisan wa ima nansai desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お兄さんは今何歳ですか？
examplePolite.english: How old is your brother now?

items.notes: Shop staff and strangers also use it to call a young man.

items.use: Your own older sister when talking to others; someone else's is oneesan.

example.romaji: ane ga raigetsu kekkon suru n da
example.ja: 姉が来月結婚するんだ
example.english: My big sister's getting married next month.

examplePolite.romaji: ane wa kangoshi desu
examplePolite.ja: 姉は看護師です
examplePolite.english: My older sister is a nurse.

items.notes: To her face you say oneechan or her name, never ane.

items.use: Someone else's older sister, or what you call your own to her face.

example.ja: お姉さんって優しいね
example.english: Your sister's so kind.

examplePolite.romaji: oneesan wa doko ni sunde imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お姉さんはどこに住んでいますか？
examplePolite.english: Where does your sister live?

items.notes: Also a friendly way to call a young woman, such as shop staff.

blocks.label: Siblings and younger ones
blocks.rationale: Lets you say how many siblings you have and which ones.
blocks.interference: otouto (younger brother) starts like otousan (father).

items.use: Brothers and sisters in general; the kanji says brothers but it covers sisters too.

example.ja: 兄弟は何人いるの？
example.english: How many brothers and sisters do you have?

examplePolite.romaji: kyoudai ga futari imasu
examplePolite.ja: 兄弟が二人います
examplePolite.english: I have two siblings.

items.notes: Someone else's siblings are gokyoudai; hitorikko means an only child.

items.use: Your own younger sister; someone else's is imoutosan.

example.ja: 妹が風邪ひいちゃった
example.english: My little sister caught a cold.

examplePolite.romaji: imouto wa koukousei desu
examplePolite.ja: 妹は高校生です
examplePolite.english: My younger sister is in high school.

items.use: Your own younger brother; someone else's is otoutosan.

example.ja: 弟とゲームしてた
example.english: I was playing games with my little brother.

examplePolite.romaji: otouto wa daigakusei desu
examplePolite.ja: 弟は大学生です
examplePolite.english: My younger brother is a university student.

items.notes: Don't mix it up with otousan (father).

items.use: Someone else's younger sister.

example.ja: 妹さんは今いくつ？
example.english: How old's your little sister now?

examplePolite.romaji: imoutosan wa ogenki desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 妹さんはお元気ですか？
examplePolite.english: How is your sister?

blocks.label: Face
blocks.rationale: Lets you name the parts of your face.
blocks.interference: hana (nose) sounds like hana (flower); me is one short sound and easy to miss.

example.ja: 花粉で目がかゆい
example.english: My eyes are itchy from pollen.

examplePolite.romaji: kafun de me ga kayui desu
examplePolite.ja: 花粉で目がかゆいです
examplePolite.english: My eyes are itchy from pollen.

items.notes: Also an experience: hidoi me ni atta means I had an awful time.

example.ja: ちょっと顔洗ってくるね
example.english: I'll just go wash my face.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto kao o aratte kimasu
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと顔を洗ってきます
examplePolite.english: I'll just go wash my face.

items.notes: Kao o dasu means to show up somewhere.

example.ja: はい、口大きく開けて
example.english: Okay, open your mouth wide.

examplePolite.romaji: kuchi o ookiku akete kudasai
examplePolite.ja: 口を大きく開けてください
examplePolite.english: Please open your mouth wide.

items.notes: Also how someone talks: kuchi ga warui means sharp-tongued.

example.ja: 耳に水入っちゃった
example.english: I got water in my ear.

examplePolite.romaji: mimi ni mizu ga haitte shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 耳に水が入ってしまいました
examplePolite.english: I got water in my ear.

items.notes: Mimi ga tooi means hard of hearing.

example.ja: 風邪で鼻が詰まってる
example.english: My nose is blocked from a cold.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze de hana ga tsumatte imasu
examplePolite.ja: 風邪で鼻が詰まっています
examplePolite.english: My nose is blocked from a cold.

items.notes: Same sound as hana (flower). A runny nose is hanamizu.

blocks.label: Head and shoulders
blocks.rationale: Lets you say where it hurts above the chest.
blocks.interference: kami (hair) sounds like kami (paper, god).

example.ja: 今日はずっと頭痛い
example.english: I've had a headache all day.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa zutto atama ga itai desu
examplePolite.ja: 今日はずっと頭が痛いです
examplePolite.english: I've had a headache all day.

items.notes: Atama ii means smart; atama ni kuru means to get mad.

example.ja: あれ、髪短くした？
example.english: Oh, did you cut your hair short?

examplePolite.romaji: kami o mijikaku shimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 髪を短くしましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you cut your hair short?

items.notes: Same sound as kami (paper; god). Body hair is ke.

example.romaji: sumaho no misugi de kubi ga itai
example.ja: スマホの見すぎで首が痛い
example.english: My neck hurts from too much phone time.

examplePolite.romaji: sumaho no misugi de kubi ga itai desu
examplePolite.ja: スマホの見すぎで首が痛いです
examplePolite.english: My neck hurts from too much phone time.

items.notes: Kubi ni naru means to get fired.

example.ja: 仕事で肩凝ったなあ
example.english: My shoulders are so stiff from work.

examplePolite.romaji: shigoto de kata ga kotte imasu
examplePolite.ja: 仕事で肩が凝っています
examplePolite.english: My shoulders are stiff from work.

items.notes: Kata ga koru, stiff shoulders, is a very common complaint.

blocks.label: Hands and feet
blocks.rationale: Lets you name your limbs and fingers.
blocks.interference: ashi covers both leg and foot; te often covers the arm too.

example.romaji: gohan no mae ni te aratta?
example.ja: ご飯の前に手洗った？
example.english: Did you wash your hands before eating?

examplePolite.romaji: gohan no mae ni te o aratte kudasai
examplePolite.ja: ご飯の前に手を洗ってください
examplePolite.english: Please wash your hands before eating.

items.notes: Also help: te ga tarinai means short-handed.

example.ja: 正座してて足がしびれた
example.english: My legs went numb from kneeling.

examplePolite.romaji: seiza o shite ite ashi ga shibiremashita
examplePolite.ja: 正座をしていて足がしびれました
examplePolite.english: My legs went numb from kneeling.

items.notes: One word for both leg and foot; context decides.

example.ja: 包丁で指切っちゃった
example.english: I cut my finger with the kitchen knife.

examplePolite.romaji: houchou de yubi o kitte shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 包丁で指を切ってしまいました
examplePolite.english: I cut my finger with the kitchen knife.

items.notes: Toes are ashi no yubi; the thumb is oyayubi.

example.ja: 荷物重くて腕が疲れた
example.english: My arms are tired from the heavy bags.

examplePolite.romaji: nimotsu ga omokute ude ga tsukaremashita
examplePolite.ja: 荷物が重くて腕が疲れました
examplePolite.english: My arms are tired from the heavy bags.

items.notes: Also skill: ude ga ii means skilled.

blocks.label: Belly, back and chest
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about hunger and aches in the body.
blocks.interference: onaka is the everyday word; hara is blunt and mostly male.

items.use: Onaka suita means I'm hungry; onaka ippai means I'm full.

example.ja: ああ、お腹すいたなあ
example.english: Man, I'm hungry.

examplePolite.romaji: onaka ga sukimashita ne
examplePolite.ja: お腹がすきましたね
examplePolite.english: I'm getting hungry.

items.notes: Onaka ga itai means I have a stomachache.

example.ja: ちょっと背中かいてくれない？
example.english: Can you scratch my back?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto senaka o kaite moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと背中をかいてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Could you scratch my back?

items.notes: The lower back is koshi.

example.romaji: kyuu ni mune ga kurushiku natta
example.ja: 急に胸が苦しくなった
example.english: My chest suddenly got tight.

examplePolite.romaji: kyuu ni mune ga kurushiku narimashita
examplePolite.ja: 急に胸が苦しくなりました
examplePolite.english: My chest suddenly got tight.

items.notes: Also feelings: mune ga itai can mean heartache.

items.use: Blunt, mostly male word for onaka; hara hetta means I'm starving.

example.ja: 腹減った、なんか食おうぜ
example.english: I'm starving, let's eat something.

items.notes: Hara ga tatsu means to get angry.

blocks.label: I and you
blocks.rationale: Lets you say I and you in casual talk.
blocks.interference: ore is men-only and atashi women-leaning; anata and kimi can sound cold or bossy where a name would do.

items.use: Men's everyday 'I' with friends and family; switch to watashi or boku in polite talk.

example.romaji: ore mo issho ni iku yo
example.ja: 俺も一緒に行くよ
example.english: I'll come with you.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi mo issho ni ikimasu
examplePolite.ja: 私も一緒に行きます
examplePolite.english: I'll come with you.

items.use: Sounds distant or pointed face to face; Japanese usually use the person's name instead.

example.ja: あなたはどう思う？
example.english: What do you think?

examplePolite.romaji: anata wa dou omoimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あなたはどう思いますか？
examplePolite.english: What do you think?

items.notes: Some wives call their husband anata, like 'dear'.

items.use: Soft, casual 'I', mostly used by women.

example.romaji: atashi wa betsu ni ii kedo
example.ja: あたしは別にいいけど
example.english: I don't really mind, though.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa betsu ni kamaimasen
examplePolite.ja: 私は別に構いません
examplePolite.english: I don't really mind.

items.use: Said to friends, partners or juniors, mostly by men and bosses; everywhere in songs.

example.ja: 君も一緒に来る？
example.english: Are you coming too?

items.notes: Sounds condescending to someone older or senior.

blocks.label: He, she, that person
blocks.rationale: Lets you point to and talk about other people.
blocks.interference: kare and kanojo usually mean boyfriend and girlfriend, not just he and she.

items.use: The everyday way to say he or she about someone over there or not present.

example.ja: ねえ、あの人誰？
example.english: Hey, who's that?

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa dare desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの人は誰ですか？
examplePolite.english: Who is that person?

items.notes: Some wives say ano hito for their husband.

items.use: In casual talk it usually means girlfriend; as 'she' it can sound distant.

example.romaji: ima kanojo to ka iru no?
example.ja: 今彼女とかいるの？
example.english: Got a girlfriend at the moment?

examplePolite.romaji: ima kanojo wa imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今彼女はいますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have a girlfriend at the moment?

items.use: In casual talk it often means boyfriend; for 'he', people usually use the name or ano hito.

example.romaji: senshuu kare to wakareta n da
example.ja: 先週彼と別れたんだ
example.english: I broke up with my boyfriend last week.

examplePolite.romaji: senshuu kare to wakaremashita
examplePolite.ja: 先週彼と別れました
examplePolite.english: I broke up with my boyfriend last week.

items.notes: Kareshi is the plainer word for boyfriend; they is karera.

items.use: Points at someone beside you or in a photo.

example.ja: 写真のこの人、知ってる？
example.english: Do you know this person in the photo?

examplePolite.romaji: shashin no kono hito o shitte imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 写真のこの人を知っていますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you know this person in the photo?

items.use: Refers back to someone just mentioned, or someone near the listener.

example.romaji: sono hito, namae nante iu no?
example.ja: その人、名前何て言うの？
example.english: What's that person's name?

examplePolite.romaji: sono hito no namae wa nan desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: その人の名前は何ですか？
examplePolite.english: What's that person's name?

items.use: For a child or a young person, often a girl; warm or neutral.

example.ja: あの子、すごくかわいいね
example.english: That girl's really cute.

examplePolite.romaji: ano ko wa totemo kawaii desu ne
examplePolite.ja: あの子はとてもかわいいですね
examplePolite.english: That girl is very cute.

blocks.label: Saying we
blocks.rationale: Lets you say we at different levels of casualness.
blocks.interference: oretachi is men's casual talk; watashitachi works for everyone.

items.use: Neutral 'we', fine anywhere; men say oretachi or bokutachi in casual talk.

example.romaji: watashitachi mo issho ni ikou yo
example.ja: 私たちも一緒に行こうよ
example.english: Let's go along too.

examplePolite.romaji: watashitachi mo issho ni ikimashou
examplePolite.ja: 私たちも一緒に行きましょう
examplePolite.english: Let's go along too.

example.ja: 俺たちも行っていい？
example.english: Can we come too?

examplePolite.romaji: watashitachi mo itte ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 私たちも行っていいですか？
examplePolite.english: May we come too?

items.use: Gentler male 'we'; boys say it, and men use it in polite-ish talk.

example.romaji: bokutachi, onaji kurasu da yo ne
example.ja: 僕たち、同じクラスだよね
example.english: We're in the same class, right?

examplePolite.romaji: bokutachi wa onaji kurasu desu
examplePolite.ja: 僕たちは同じクラスです
examplePolite.english: We're in the same class.

blocks.label: Japan, nationality, language
blocks.rationale: Say who is Japanese, what you speak, and build any nationality or language.
blocks.interference: -jin is the person, -go the language; English is eigo, not igirisugo.

items.use: nippon is the formal or sporty version, as on national teams.

example.ja: 日本来てどれぐらい？
example.english: How long have you been in Japan?

examplePolite.romaji: nihon ni kite dore gurai desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 日本に来てどれぐらいですか？
examplePolite.english: How long have you been in Japan?

example.romaji: kare, nihonjin ja nai n da.
example.ja: 彼、日本人じゃないんだ。
example.english: Oh, he isn't Japanese.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa nihonjin ja nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は日本人じゃないんです。
examplePolite.english: He isn't Japanese, actually.

example.ja: 英語で言ってもいい？
example.english: Can I say it in English?

examplePolite.romaji: eigo de itte mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 英語で言ってもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: May I say it in English?

items.notes: Not igirisugo, even though English comes from igirisu.

items.use: Add to a country for nationality: amerikajin, kankokujin.

example.ja: 彼、アメリカ人だよ。
example.english: He's American.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa amerikajin desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はアメリカ人です。
examplePolite.english: He is American.

items.notes: nanijin? is blunt; doko kara kita no? is friendlier.

items.use: Add to a country for its language: nihongo, chuugokugo, kankokugo.

example.ja: 韓国語も話せるの？
example.english: You can speak Korean too?

examplePolite.romaji: kankokugo mo hanasemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 韓国語も話せますか？
examplePolite.english: Can you speak Korean as well?

items.notes: nanigo? = what language?

blocks.label: Building bigger numbers
blocks.rationale: Lets you say any number up to 9,999.
blocks.interference: Juuni (12) and nijuu (20) swap the same two parts.

items.use: Teens are ten plus the digit, with the same yon, nana and kyuu choices as the digits.

example.ja: 十一時まで開いてるよ。
example.english: It's open till eleven.

examplePolite.romaji: juuichiji made aite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 十一時まで開いています。
examplePolite.english: It's open until eleven.

items.notes: Juuyon is the usual 14; juushichi and juunana are both common for 17.

items.english: twenty (and the tens: digit times ten)
items.use: Tens put the digit before juu, and use yon, nana and kyuu.

example.ja: もう二十五だよ。
example.english: I'm already twenty-five.

examplePolite.romaji: mou nijuugosai desu.
examplePolite.ja: もう二十五歳です。
examplePolite.english: I'm already twenty-five.

items.notes: Age 20 is usually hatachi rather than nijussai.

items.use: Hyaku alone means one hundred; no ichi in front.

example.ja: 百円で買えるよ。
example.english: You can get it for a hundred yen.

examplePolite.romaji: hyaku en de kaemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 百円で買えます。
examplePolite.english: You can buy it for a hundred yen.

items.notes: Changes after 3, 6 and 8: sanbyaku, roppyaku, happyaku. A hyaku en shoppu is a 100-yen shop.

items.use: Sen alone means one thousand; issen is only heard inside issenman (ten million).

example.ja: 千円貸して。
example.english: Lend me a thousand yen.

examplePolite.romaji: sen en kashite kuremasen ka.
examplePolite.ja: 千円貸してくれませんか。
examplePolite.english: Could you lend me a thousand yen?

items.notes: Changes after 3 and 8: sanzen, hassen. How many thousand is nanzen.

blocks.label: Changed hundreds and thousands
blocks.rationale: Lets you say prices like 300 or 8,000 yen correctly.
blocks.interference: Saying the regular rokuhyaku or hachisen instead of the changed forms.

example.ja: これ、三百円だよ。
example.english: This is three hundred yen.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa sanbyaku en desu.
examplePolite.ja: これは三百円です。
examplePolite.english: This is three hundred yen.

items.notes: Not sanhyaku: h turns to b after san. Nanbyaku (how many hundred) changes the same way.

example.ja: 切符、六百円だった。
example.english: The ticket was six hundred yen.

examplePolite.romaji: kippu wa roppyaku en deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 切符は六百円でした。
examplePolite.english: The ticket was six hundred yen.

items.notes: Not rokuhyaku: roku shortens to rop- and h becomes p.

example.romaji: ranchi, happyaku en de yasui ne.
example.ja: ランチ、八百円で安いね。
example.english: Lunch is cheap at eight hundred yen.

examplePolite.romaji: ranchi wa happyaku en de yasui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ランチは八百円で安いですね。
examplePolite.english: Lunch is cheap at eight hundred yen.

items.notes: Not hachihyaku: hachi shortens to hap- and h becomes p.

example.ja: 三千円で足りる？
example.english: Is three thousand yen enough?

examplePolite.romaji: sanzen en de tarimasu ka.
examplePolite.ja: 三千円で足りますか。
examplePolite.english: Will three thousand yen be enough?

items.notes: Not sansen: s turns to z after san.

example.ja: ホテル、八千円だったよ。
example.english: The hotel was eight thousand yen.

examplePolite.romaji: hoteru wa hassen en deshita.
examplePolite.ja: ホテルは八千円でした。
examplePolite.english: The hotel was eight thousand yen.

items.notes: Not hachisen. Rokusen (6,000) stays regular.

blocks.label: Big numbers in man
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about rent, salaries and big prices.
blocks.interference: English counts in thousands; 100,000 is juuman, not hyakusen.

items.use: Japanese groups big numbers in man (10,000), not thousands, and always says ichiman, never man alone.

example.ja: 一万円札しかない。
example.english: I've only got a ten-thousand-yen note.

examplePolite.romaji: ichiman en satsu shika arimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 一万円札しかありません。
examplePolite.english: I only have a ten-thousand-yen note.

items.notes: Count up in man: niman is 20,000, goman is 50,000.

items.use: Ten man; prices and rent in this range are said in man.

example.ja: 家賃、十万ぐらいだよ。
example.english: Rent's about a hundred thousand yen.

examplePolite.romaji: yachin wa juuman en gurai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 家賃は十万円ぐらいです。
examplePolite.english: The rent is about a hundred thousand yen.

items.notes: Not hyakusen. Two hundred thousand is nijuuman.

items.use: A hundred man; there is no separate word for million.

example.ja: 百万円当たったら何する？
example.english: What would you do if you won a million yen?

examplePolite.romaji: hyakuman en atattara nani o shimasu ka.
examplePolite.ja: 百万円当たったら何をしますか。
examplePolite.english: What would you do if you won a million yen?

items.notes: Ten million is issenman, with sen shortened to issen.

items.use: The next unit after man: ten thousand man is ichioku.

example.romaji: ichioku en atte mo tarinai yo.
example.ja: 一億円あっても足りないよ。
example.english: Even a hundred million yen wouldn't be enough.

examplePolite.romaji: ichioku en atte mo tarimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 一億円あっても足りません。
examplePolite.english: Even a hundred million yen wouldn't be enough.

items.notes: The classic 'fortune' number in lotteries and dreams. A billion is juuoku.

blocks.label: Asking how many
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask how many, say 'a few' and go through things one by one.
blocks.interference: Ikutsu asks how many; ikutsuka means a few.

items.use: Asks how many things with no special counter, and a child's or friend's age.

example.ja: いくつ要る？
example.english: How many do you need?

examplePolite.romaji: ikutsu irimasu ka.
examplePolite.ja: いくつ要りますか。
examplePolite.english: How many do you need?

items.notes: To ask an adult's age politely, say oikutsu desu ka. Ikura asks how much money.

items.use: A vague small number of things; for people use nannin ka.

example.ja: いくつか質問していい？
example.english: Can I ask a few questions?

examplePolite.romaji: ikutsuka shitsumon shite mo ii desu ka.
examplePolite.ja: いくつか質問してもいいですか。
examplePolite.english: May I ask a few questions?

items.notes: A statement, not a question: the ka makes it vague, like 'some'.

items.use: Stresses going through things one at a time, carefully.

example.ja: 一つ一つチェックしたよ。
example.english: I checked each one.

examplePolite.romaji: hitotsu hitotsu chekku shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 一つ一つチェックしました。
examplePolite.english: I checked them one by one.

items.notes: For people, it's hitori hitori.

blocks.label: Both, each, only one
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about both people, each person, a lone person and the headcount.
blocks.interference: Hitori hitori (each person) vs hitotsu hitotsu (each thing).

example.ja: 二人とも元気だよ。
example.english: They're both doing well.

examplePolite.romaji: futari tomo genki desu.
examplePolite.ja: 二人とも元気です。
examplePolite.english: They are both well.

items.notes: For two things, both is ryouhou. Three people works the same: sannin tomo.

items.use: Stresses every individual, not the group.

example.romaji: hitori hitori kangae ga chigau yo.
example.ja: 一人一人考えが違うよ。
example.english: Everyone thinks differently.

examplePolite.romaji: hitori hitori kangae ga chigaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 一人一人考えが違います。
examplePolite.english: Each person has different ideas.

items.notes: For things, it's hitotsu hitotsu.

items.use: Tatta stresses how few, often with a sad or surprised tone.

example.romaji: kita no wa tatta hitori datta.
example.ja: 来たのはたった一人だった。
example.english: Only one person showed up.

examplePolite.romaji: kita no wa tatta hitori deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 来たのはたった一人でした。
examplePolite.english: Only one person came.

items.notes: Tatta works with any number: tatta hyaku en = a mere 100 yen.

items.use: Used for bookings, parties and group plans.

example.ja: 人数確認しておくね。
example.english: I'll check the headcount.

examplePolite.romaji: ninzuu o kakunin shite okimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 人数を確認しておきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll confirm the number of people.

items.notes: Said ninzuu, with z, not ninsuu.

blocks.label: Prices and shop counters
blocks.rationale: Lets you say prices and buy or order things by the piece, bottle, sheet or cup.
blocks.interference: -hon and -hai share the same changes (ippon/ippai, sanbon/sanbai); 4 yen is yoen.

items.use: After the number: ichien, nien, san'en, yoen, goen, rokuen, nanaen, hachien, kyuuen, juuen; to ask a price, say ikura (or nan'en).

example.romaji: zenbu de nisen en gurai da yo.
example.ja: 全部で二千円ぐらいだよ。
example.english: It's about 2,000 yen altogether.

examplePolite.romaji: zenbu de nisen en gurai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 全部で二千円ぐらいです。
examplePolite.english: It comes to about 2,000 yen altogether.

items.notes: Watch 4 yen (yoen) and 9 yen (kyuuen). 10,000 yen is ichiman'en, not juusen'en.

items.use: For small or chunky things like eggs, apples and sweets: ikko, niko, sanko, yonko, goko, rokko, nanako, hakko, kyuuko, jukko; how many is nanko.

example.ja: 卵、一個残ってるよ。
example.english: There's one egg left.

examplePolite.romaji: tamago ga ikko nokotte imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 卵が一個残っています。
examplePolite.english: There's one egg left.

items.notes: Hitotsu, futatsu ... works for the same things and is the safe default.

items.english: long thin things (counter): bottles, pens, umbrellas
items.use: Changes with the number: ippon, nihon, sanbon, yonhon, gohon, roppon, nanahon, happon, kyuuhon, juppon; how many is nanbon.

example.ja: ビール、もう一本飲む？
example.english: Want another bottle of beer?

examplePolite.romaji: biiru, mou ippon nomimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ビール、もう一本飲みますか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like another bottle of beer?

items.notes: Also counts films, phone calls and trains.

items.english: flat things (counter): sheets, tickets, plates, shirts
items.use: No sound changes: ichimai, nimai, sanmai, yonmai ... juumai; how many is nanmai.

example.ja: 紙、一枚もらっていい？
example.english: Can I have a sheet of paper?

examplePolite.romaji: kami o ichimai moratte mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 紙を一枚もらってもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: May I have a sheet of paper?

items.notes: Also counts photos and slices of bread or pizza.

items.use: Same changes as -hon: ippai, nihai, sanbai, yonhai, gohai, roppai, nanahai, happai, kyuuhai, juppai; how many is nanbai.

example.ja: コーヒー、もう一杯飲もうか。
example.english: Shall we have another cup of coffee?

examplePolite.romaji: koohii, mou ippai nomimashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: コーヒー、もう一杯飲みましょうか。
examplePolite.english: Shall we have another cup of coffee?

items.notes: Ippai on its own also means 'full' or 'lots'.

blocks.label: How many times
blocks.rationale: Lets you say how often something happened and ask how many times.
blocks.interference: -kai and -do mean the same here; ikkai is also 'ground floor'.

items.use: ikkai, nikai, sankai, yonkai, gokai, rokkai, nanakai, hakkai, kyuukai, jukkai; mou ikkai = one more time.

example.ja: ごめん、もう一回言って。
example.english: Sorry, say that again.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, mou ikkai itte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、もう一回言ってください。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, could you say that again?

items.notes: Sounds the same as -kai for floors, so ikkai is also 'ground floor'. -do means the same and is a bit more formal.

items.use: Nankai mo = many times, over and over.

example.ja: この映画、何回見た？
example.english: How many times have you seen this movie?

examplePolite.romaji: kono eiga, nankai mimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: この映画、何回見ましたか？
examplePolite.english: How many times have you seen this movie?

items.notes: In a building, nankai (or nangai) also asks 'which floor'.

items.use: Like -kai but a bit more formal, with no sound changes: ichido, nido, sando ... juudo; mou ichido = once more.

example.romaji: ichido ano mise ni itte mitai na.
example.ja: 一度あの店に行ってみたいな。
example.english: I'd like to try that place sometime.

examplePolite.romaji: ichido ano mise ni itte mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 一度あの店に行ってみたいです。
examplePolite.english: I'd like to try that place sometime.

items.notes: Ichido alone often means 'sometime, at least once'. Also degrees: sanjuu-do = 30 degrees.

items.use: Mostly heard as nando mo, 'again and again', often with some annoyance.

example.ja: 何度も言ったでしょ。
example.english: I've told you again and again.

examplePolite.romaji: nando mo iimashita yo.
examplePolite.ja: 何度も言いましたよ。
examplePolite.english: I've told you many times.

items.notes: A little more formal than nankai.

blocks.label: Minutes and roughly when
blocks.rationale: Lets you give exact minutes, rough times, and how long ago.
blocks.interference: -mae means both 'to the hour' and 'ago'; goro is for times, gurai for amounts.

items.use: Many become -pun: ippun, nifun, sanpun, yonpun, gofun, roppun, nanafun, happun, kyuufun, juppun; what minute or how many is nanpun.

example.ja: あと十分で着くよ。
example.english: I'll be there in ten minutes.

examplePolite.romaji: ato juppun de tsukimasu.
examplePolite.ja: あと十分で着きます。
examplePolite.english: I'll arrive in ten minutes.

items.notes: Thirty past is usually han. -fun also gives lengths of time: juppun kakaru = takes ten minutes.

items.use: After a time or date: sanji goro, raishuu goro; for amounts use gurai instead.

example.romaji: kyou wa rokuji goro kaeru ne.
example.ja: 今日は六時ごろ帰るね。
example.english: I'll be home around six today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa rokuji goro kaerimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は六時ごろ帰ります。
examplePolite.english: I'll be home around six today.

items.notes: Goro and goro ni both work: rokuji goro (ni) kaeru.

items.use: After a time: juuji sugi = just after ten; sanji juppun sugi = ten past three.

example.romaji: kaetta no, juuniji sugi datta yo.
example.ja: 帰ったの、十二時過ぎだったよ。
example.english: I got home after midnight.

examplePolite.romaji: kaetta no wa juuniji sugi deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 帰ったのは十二時過ぎでした。
examplePolite.english: I got home after midnight.

items.notes: After a verb stem, -sugi means 'too much': tabesugi = overeating.

items.use: After a time for 'to' (goji juppun mae = ten to five), after a length of time for 'ago' (mikka mae = three days ago).

example.ja: 十分前に出たよ。
example.english: I left ten minutes ago.

examplePolite.romaji: juppun mae ni demashita.
examplePolite.ja: 十分前に出ました。
examplePolite.english: I left ten minutes ago.

items.notes: Mae alone also means 'front': eki no mae = in front of the station.

blocks.label: How long it takes
blocks.rationale: Lets you say how many hours, minutes, seconds or weeks something lasts.
blocks.interference: niji (two o'clock) vs nijikan (two hours).

items.use: ichijikan, nijikan, sanjikan, yojikan, gojikan, rokujikan, nanajikan (or shichijikan), hachijikan, kujikan, juujikan; how long is nanjikan.

example.romaji: densha de nijikan gurai kakaru yo.
example.ja: 電車で二時間ぐらいかかるよ。
example.english: It takes about two hours by train.

examplePolite.romaji: densha de nijikan gurai kakarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 電車で二時間ぐらいかかります。
examplePolite.english: It takes about two hours by train.

items.notes: Jikan alone means 'time': jikan ga nai = no time.

items.use: Stresses how long: juppunkan = for ten minutes; in speech plain -fun often does the same job.

example.ja: じゃあ、五分間だけ休もうか。
example.english: Okay, let's rest for just five minutes.

examplePolite.romaji: dewa, gofunkan dake yasumimashou.
examplePolite.ja: では、五分間だけ休みましょう。
examplePolite.english: Then let's rest for just five minutes.

items.notes: Same sound changes as -fun: ippunkan, sanpunkan, roppunkan, juppunkan.

items.use: No sound changes: ichibyou, nibyou ... juubyou; how many is nanbyou.

example.ja: あと三十秒で始まるよ。
example.english: It starts in thirty seconds.

examplePolite.romaji: ato sanjuubyou de hajimarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: あと三十秒で始まります。
examplePolite.english: It starts in thirty seconds.

items.notes: For 'just a second', people say chotto matte, not byou.

items.use: isshuukan, nishuukan, sanshuukan, yonshuukan, goshuukan, rokushuukan, nanashuukan, hasshuukan, kyuushuukan, jusshuukan; how many is nanshuukan.

example.ja: 一週間ぐらい休み取るつもり。
example.english: I'm planning to take about a week off.

examplePolite.romaji: isshuukan gurai yasumi o toru tsumori desu.
examplePolite.ja: 一週間ぐらい休みを取るつもりです。
examplePolite.english: I'm planning to take about a week off.

items.notes: Raishuu (next week) and senshuu (last week) don't take -kan.

blocks.label: Weekdays and days off
blocks.rationale: Lets you use the short day names and talk about workdays versus days off.
blocks.interference: Kyuujitsu (any day off) vs shukujitsu (public holiday).

items.use: Any day name can drop -bi in speech: getsuyou, kayou, suiyou, mokuyou, kin'you, doyou.

example.ja: 日曜なら空いてるよ。
example.english: Sunday works for me.

examplePolite.romaji: nichiyou nara aite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 日曜なら空いています。
examplePolite.english: I'm free on Sunday.

items.notes: Donichi means Saturday and Sunday together.

items.use: Pairs with shuumatsu (weekend); opening hours and train times often differ between them.

example.romaji: heijitsu wa isogashii kara, shuumatsu ni shiyou.
example.ja: 平日は忙しいから、週末にしよう。
example.english: Weekdays are busy, so let's do the weekend.

examplePolite.romaji: heijitsu wa isogashii node, shuumatsu ni shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 平日は忙しいので、週末にしましょう。
examplePolite.english: I'm busy on weekdays, so let's make it the weekend.

items.use: Any non-working day, weekends included; yasumi is the more everyday word.

example.ja: 休日は何してるの？
example.english: What do you do on your days off?

examplePolite.romaji: kyuujitsu wa nani o shite imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 休日は何をしていますか？
examplePolite.english: What do you do on your days off?

items.notes: A national public holiday is shukujitsu.

blocks.label: The 1st to 5th
blocks.rationale: Lets you say the first five dates and spans of two to five days.
blocks.interference: Tsuitachi is only the date; a day long is ichinichi.

items.use: Only the date; a length of one day is ichinichi.

example.romaji: raigetsu no tsuitachi ni hikkosu n da.
example.ja: 来月の一日に引っ越すんだ。
example.english: I'm moving on the 1st of next month.

examplePolite.romaji: raigetsu no tsuitachi ni hikkoshimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 来月の一日に引っ越します。
examplePolite.english: I'm moving on the 1st of next month.

items.use: Same word for the date and for a two-day span.

example.romaji: shigatsu futsuka ga tanjoubi nan da.
example.ja: 四月二日が誕生日なんだ。
example.english: My birthday's April 2nd.

examplePolite.romaji: shigatsu futsuka ga tanjoubi desu.
examplePolite.ja: 四月二日が誕生日です。
examplePolite.english: My birthday is April 2nd.

items.notes: Futsukayoi (hangover) is built on it.

example.ja: 三日で終わると思う。
example.english: I think it'll be done in three days.

examplePolite.romaji: mikka de owaru to omoimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 三日で終わると思います。
examplePolite.english: I think it will be finished in three days.

items.notes: Don't mix with muika (the 6th).

example.ja: 四日の午後はどう？
example.english: How about the afternoon of the 4th?

examplePolite.romaji: yokka no gogo wa ikaga desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 四日の午後はいかがですか？
examplePolite.english: Would the afternoon of the 4th work?

items.notes: Don't mix with youka (the 8th): yokka has the short pause, youka the long o.

example.ja: 五日までに教えて。
example.english: Let me know by the 5th.

examplePolite.romaji: itsuka made ni oshiete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 五日までに教えてください。
examplePolite.english: Please let me know by the 5th.

items.notes: Sounds the same as itsuka (someday); context tells them apart.

blocks.label: The 6th to 10th
blocks.rationale: Lets you say the 6th to the 10th and spans of six to ten days.
blocks.interference: Youka (8th) vs yokka (4th); muika (6th) vs mikka (3rd).

example.ja: 六日まで出張なんだ。
example.english: I'm on a business trip until the 6th.

examplePolite.romaji: muika made shutchou desu.
examplePolite.ja: 六日まで出張です。
examplePolite.english: I'm away on business until the 6th.

items.notes: Never rokunichi.

example.ja: 七日の夜、空いてる？
example.english: Are you free the night of the 7th?

examplePolite.romaji: nanoka no yoru wa aite imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 七日の夜は空いていますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you free on the evening of the 7th?

items.notes: Nanuka is also heard.

example.romaji: youka made ni henji suru ne.
example.ja: 八日までに返事するね。
example.english: I'll get back to you by the 8th.

examplePolite.romaji: youka made ni henji shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 八日までに返事します。
examplePolite.english: I'll reply by the 8th.

items.notes: Don't mix with yokka (the 4th).

example.romaji: kokonoka wa tomodachi no kekkonshiki nan da.
example.ja: 九日は友達の結婚式なんだ。
example.english: The 9th is my friend's wedding.

examplePolite.romaji: kokonoka wa tomodachi no kekkonshiki desu.
examplePolite.ja: 九日は友達の結婚式です。
examplePolite.english: The 9th is my friend's wedding.

example.ja: 十日に帰ってくるよ。
example.english: I'll be back on the 10th.

examplePolite.romaji: tooka ni kaette kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 十日に帰ってきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll be back on the 10th.

items.notes: Never juunichi.

blocks.label: Other dates
blocks.rationale: Lets you say any date in the month and ask what the date is.
blocks.interference: Hatsuka (20th) vs futsuka (2nd).

items.use: Every date not on the irregular list is just the number plus nichi; 17th and 19th use shichi and ku.

example.ja: 十五日から夏休みだよ。
example.english: Summer break starts on the 15th.

examplePolite.romaji: juugonichi kara natsuyasumi desu.
examplePolite.ja: 十五日から夏休みです。
examplePolite.english: Summer break starts on the 15th.

items.use: Like the 4th it takes yokka, not yonnichi.

example.romaji: barentain wa nigatsu juuyokka da yo.
example.ja: バレンタインは二月十四日だよ。
example.english: Valentine's Day is February 14th.

examplePolite.romaji: barentain wa nigatsu juuyokka desu.
examplePolite.ja: バレンタインは二月十四日です。
examplePolite.english: Valentine's Day is February 14th.

items.use: Not nijuunichi.

example.ja: 二十日に家賃払わなきゃ。
example.english: I have to pay rent on the 20th.

examplePolite.romaji: hatsuka ni yachin o harawanai to ikemasen.
examplePolite.ja: 二十日に家賃を払わないといけません。
examplePolite.english: I have to pay the rent on the 20th.

items.notes: Don't mix with futsuka (the 2nd).

items.use: Any date ending in 4 uses yokka: 4th, 14th, 24th.

example.romaji: nijuuyokka no yoru wa dou suru?
example.ja: 二十四日の夜はどうする？
example.english: What are you doing the night of the 24th?

examplePolite.romaji: nijuuyokka no yoru wa dou shimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 二十四日の夜はどうしますか？
examplePolite.english: What are your plans for the evening of the 24th?

example.ja: 会議は何日になる？
example.english: What date will the meeting be?

examplePolite.romaji: kaigi wa nannichi ni narimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 会議は何日になりますか？
examplePolite.english: What date will the meeting be on?

items.notes: Add -kan to ask only the length: nannichikan.

blocks.label: Counting days
blocks.rationale: Lets you say how many days something lasts.
blocks.interference: Ichinichi (one day) vs tsuitachi (the 1st).

example.ja: 昨日は一日中寝てた。
example.english: I slept all day yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa ichinichijuu nete imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日は一日中寝ていました。
examplePolite.english: I slept all day yesterday.

items.use: Takes the irregular day forms: futsukakan, mikkakan, yokkakan, tookakan; one day is ichinichi, not tsuitachi.

example.ja: 三日間ずっと雨だった。
example.english: It rained for three days straight.

examplePolite.romaji: mikkakan zutto ame deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 三日間ずっと雨でした。
examplePolite.english: It rained for three days straight.

items.notes: -kan is often dropped: mikka yasunda (took three days off).

items.use: A bit formal; in casual talk people often say nisannichi (two or three days).

example.ja: 数日で治るって。
example.english: They said it'll heal in a few days.

examplePolite.romaji: suujitsu de naoru sou desu.
examplePolite.ja: 数日で治るそうです。
examplePolite.english: I'm told it will heal in a few days.

blocks.label: January to June
blocks.rationale: Lets you name the first six months.
blocks.interference: April is shigatsu, never yongatsu.

example.ja: 一月はすごく寒いよ。
example.english: January is really cold.

examplePolite.romaji: ichigatsu wa totemo samui desu.
examplePolite.ja: 一月はとても寒いです。
examplePolite.english: January is very cold.

items.notes: Don't mix with shichigatsu (July) by ear.

example.romaji: nigatsu ni nihon ni iku n da.
example.ja: 二月に日本に行くんだ。
example.english: I'm going to Japan in February.

examplePolite.romaji: nigatsu ni nihon ni ikimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 二月に日本に行きます。
examplePolite.english: I'm going to Japan in February.

items.notes: Nikagetsu is two months, not February.

example.romaji: sangatsu ni sotsugyou suru n da.
example.ja: 三月に卒業するんだ。
example.english: I graduate in March.

examplePolite.romaji: sangatsu ni sotsugyou shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 三月に卒業します。
examplePolite.english: I graduate in March.

items.notes: The Japanese school and business year ends in March.

example.romaji: shigatsu kara atarashii shigoto nan da.
example.ja: 四月から新しい仕事なんだ。
example.english: I start a new job in April.

examplePolite.romaji: shigatsu kara atarashii shigoto desu.
examplePolite.ja: 四月から新しい仕事です。
examplePolite.english: I'm starting a new job in April.

items.notes: Never yongatsu.

example.romaji: gogatsu wa tenki ga ii ne.
example.ja: 五月は天気がいいね。
example.english: The weather's nice in May.

examplePolite.romaji: gogatsu wa tenki ga ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 五月は天気がいいですね。
examplePolite.english: The weather is nice in May, isn't it?

items.notes: Golden Week holidays fall at the start of May.

example.romaji: rokugatsu wa ame bakkari da yo.
example.ja: 六月は雨ばっかりだよ。
example.english: It rains all the time in June.

examplePolite.romaji: rokugatsu wa ame bakari desu.
examplePolite.ja: 六月は雨ばかりです。
examplePolite.english: It rains a lot in June.

items.notes: The rainy season (tsuyu) month.

blocks.label: July to December
blocks.rationale: Lets you name the last six months.
blocks.interference: Shichigatsu (July) sounds close to ichigatsu (January); September is kugatsu, never kyuugatsu.

example.romaji: shichigatsu no owari ni natsuyasumi ga hajimaru.
example.ja: 七月の終わりに夏休みが始まる。
example.english: Summer break starts at the end of July.

examplePolite.romaji: shichigatsu no owari ni natsuyasumi ga hajimarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 七月の終わりに夏休みが始まります。
examplePolite.english: Summer break starts at the end of July.

items.notes: Never nanagatsu; easy to mishear as ichigatsu.

example.ja: 八月は暑くて無理。
example.english: August is unbearably hot.

examplePolite.romaji: hachigatsu wa atsukute taihen desu.
examplePolite.ja: 八月は暑くて大変です。
examplePolite.english: August is really hot and hard going.

items.notes: The Obon holidays fall in mid-August.

example.romaji: kugatsu ni natte mo mada atsui ne.
example.ja: 九月になってもまだ暑いね。
example.english: It's September and still hot.

examplePolite.romaji: kugatsu ni natte mo mada atsui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 九月になってもまだ暑いですね。
examplePolite.english: It's still hot even in September, isn't it?

items.notes: Never kyuugatsu.

example.ja: 十月に引っ越しする予定。
example.english: I'm planning to move in October.

examplePolite.romaji: juugatsu ni hikkoshi suru yotei desu.
examplePolite.ja: 十月に引っ越しする予定です。
examplePolite.english: I'm planning to move in October.

example.romaji: juuichigatsu ni naru to kouyou ga kirei da yo.
example.ja: 十一月になると紅葉がきれいだよ。
example.english: In November the autumn leaves are beautiful.

examplePolite.romaji: juuichigatsu ni naru to kouyou ga kirei desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 十一月になると紅葉がきれいですよ。
examplePolite.english: The autumn leaves are beautiful in November.

example.romaji: juunigatsu wa nomikai ga ooi n da yo.
example.ja: 十二月は飲み会が多いんだよ。
example.english: There are lots of drinking parties in December.

examplePolite.romaji: juunigatsu wa nomikai ga ooi desu.
examplePolite.ja: 十二月は飲み会が多いです。
examplePolite.english: December has a lot of drinking parties.

blocks.label: Asking and counting months
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask the month and say how many months something takes.
blocks.interference: Nigatsu (February) vs nikagetsu (two months).

items.use: Months are just the number + -gatsu, except 4, 7 and 9: shigatsu, shichigatsu, kugatsu.

example.ja: 誕生日って何月だった？
example.english: What month is your birthday again?

examplePolite.romaji: tanjoubi wa nangatsu desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 誕生日は何月ですか？
examplePolite.english: What month is your birthday?

items.notes: Nankagetsu asks how many months.

items.use: ikkagetsu, nikagetsu, sankagetsu, yonkagetsu, gokagetsu, rokkagetsu, nanakagetsu, hachikagetsu (or hakkagetsu), kyuukagetsu, jukkagetsu; how many: nankagetsu.

example.romaji: nihon ni kite mada ikkagetsu da yo.
example.ja: 日本に来てまだ一か月だよ。
example.english: I've only been in Japan a month.

examplePolite.romaji: nihon ni kite mada ikkagetsu desu.
examplePolite.ja: 日本に来てまだ一か月です。
examplePolite.english: It's only been a month since I came to Japan.

items.notes: Nikagetsu (two months) and nigatsu (February) are the classic mix-up.

items.use: More natural in talk than rokkagetsu.

example.romaji: hantoshi mae ni hajimeta n da.
example.ja: 半年前に始めたんだ。
example.english: I started six months ago.

examplePolite.romaji: hantoshi mae ni hajimemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 半年前に始めました。
examplePolite.english: I started half a year ago.

blocks.label: Counting years
blocks.rationale: Lets you give a year, say how many years, and name a school year.
blocks.interference: Four years is yonen, not yonnen; nannen can mean 'what year' or 'how many years'.

items.use: ichinen, ninen, sannen, yonen, gonen, rokunen, nananen, hachinen, kyuunen, juunen; in dates, nisen nijuurokunen = 2026.

example.romaji: nihon ni kite, mou sannen ni naru.
example.ja: 日本に来て、もう三年になる。
example.english: It's been three years since I came to Japan.

examplePolite.romaji: nihon ni kite, mou sannen ni narimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 日本に来て、もう三年になります。
examplePolite.english: It's been three years since I came to Japan.

items.notes: Four years is yonen, not yonnen. For a length of time, -kan is optional: sannen or sannenkan.

items.use: Nannen umare = what year were you born, a common indirect way to ask age.

example.ja: ね、何年生まれなの？
example.english: Hey, what year were you born?

examplePolite.romaji: nannen umare desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何年生まれですか？
examplePolite.english: What year were you born?

items.notes: Nannen mo = for many years.

items.use: Stresses the span: sannenkan = for three years; same sound changes as -nen (yonenkan).

example.ja: 五年間海外に住んでた。
example.english: I lived abroad for five years.

examplePolite.romaji: gonenkan kaigai ni sunde imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 五年間海外に住んでいました。
examplePolite.english: I lived abroad for five years.

items.notes: Nenkan alone means 'per year': nenkan hyakuman en = a million yen a year.

items.english: year or grade (in school or university)
items.use: ichinensei, ninensei, sannensei, yonensei ...; daigaku yonensei = final-year university student; which year is nannensei.

example.romaji: imouto, ima koukou ninensei da yo.
example.ja: 妹、今高校二年生だよ。
example.english: My little sister's in her second year of high school.

examplePolite.romaji: imouto wa ima koukou ninensei desu.
examplePolite.ja: 妹は今高校二年生です。
examplePolite.english: My younger sister is in her second year of high school.

items.notes: The count restarts at each school: shougaku rokunensei, then chuugaku ichinensei.

blocks.label: Nearby days and nights
blocks.rationale: Lets you point to last night, tonight, the other day and two days either side of today.
blocks.interference: Ototoi (day before yesterday) vs ototoshi (year before last).

example.ja: 今夜は飲もうよ。
example.english: Let's drink tonight.

examplePolite.romaji: kon'ya wa nomimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 今夜は飲みましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's have a drink tonight.

items.notes: Konban is the more everyday word in conversation.

example.romaji: kono mae itta mise, oishikatta ne.
example.ja: この前行った店、美味しかったね。
example.english: That place we went to the other day was good, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: kono mae itta mise wa oishikatta desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この前行った店は美味しかったですね。
examplePolite.english: The restaurant we went to the other day was good, wasn't it?

items.notes: With no it means 'the last one': kono mae no shiken (the last exam).

example.ja: ゆうべは全然寝れなかった。
example.english: I couldn't sleep at all last night.

examplePolite.romaji: yuube wa zenzen nemuremasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: ゆうべは全然眠れませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I couldn't sleep at all last night.

items.notes: Kinou no yoru means the same; sakuya is the formal word.

example.ja: おとといから頭が痛い。
example.english: I've had a headache since the day before yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: ototoi kara atama ga itai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: おとといから頭が痛いんです。
examplePolite.english: I've had a headache since the day before yesterday.

items.notes: Don't mix with ototoshi (the year before last).

example.ja: あさってまでに返すね。
example.english: I'll give it back by the day after tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: asatte made ni kaeshimasu.
examplePolite.ja: あさってまでに返します。
examplePolite.english: I'll return it by the day after tomorrow.

blocks.label: Every morning, week, year
blocks.rationale: Lets you describe routines and how often things happen.
blocks.interference: Maitsuki and maitoshi have formal twins, maigetsu and mainen.

example.ja: 毎朝コーヒー飲むよ。
example.english: I have coffee every morning.

examplePolite.romaji: maiasa koohii o nomimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 毎朝コーヒーを飲みます。
examplePolite.english: I drink coffee every morning.

example.ja: 毎晩遅くまでゲームしてる。
example.english: I play games till late every night.

examplePolite.romaji: maiban osoku made geemu o shite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 毎晩遅くまでゲームをしています。
examplePolite.english: I play games until late every night.

example.romaji: maishuu kin'youbi ni au n da.
example.ja: 毎週金曜日に会うんだ。
example.english: We meet up every Friday.

examplePolite.romaji: maishuu kin'youbi ni aimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 毎週金曜日に会います。
examplePolite.english: We meet every Friday.

example.ja: 毎月二万円貯金してる。
example.english: I save 20,000 yen every month.

examplePolite.romaji: maitsuki niman en chokin shite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 毎月二万円貯金しています。
examplePolite.english: I put aside 20,000 yen every month.

items.notes: Maigetsu is the same word, more formal.

example.romaji: maitoshi natsu ni jikka ni kaeru.
example.ja: 毎年夏に実家に帰る。
example.english: I go home to my parents' every summer.

examplePolite.romaji: maitoshi natsu ni jikka ni kaerimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 毎年夏に実家に帰ります。
examplePolite.english: I go back to my parents' place every summer.

items.notes: Mainen is the same word, a bit more formal.

example.ja: 毎回同じもの頼むね。
example.english: You order the same thing every time.

examplePolite.romaji: maikai onaji mono o tanomimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 毎回同じものを頼みますね。
examplePolite.english: You always order the same thing, don't you?

blocks.label: Night and late night
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about evenings and the small hours.
blocks.interference: Yonaka and shin'ya overlap; shin'ya sounds more official.

items.use: Mostly in set words: konban (this evening), maiban, bangohan, asa kara ban made.

example.ja: 朝から晩まで働いてる。
example.english: I work from morning till night.

examplePolite.romaji: asa kara ban made hataraite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 朝から晩まで働いています。
examplePolite.english: I work from morning until night.

example.ja: 夜中に目が覚めた。
example.english: I woke up in the middle of the night.

examplePolite.romaji: yonaka ni me ga samemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 夜中に目が覚めました。
examplePolite.english: I woke up in the middle of the night.

items.notes: Mayonaka is the dead of night.

items.use: Sounds more official than yonaka; used for late shifts, late-night TV and opening hours.

example.ja: 深夜までバイトしてる。
example.english: I work my part-time job until late at night.

examplePolite.romaji: shin'ya made arubaito o shite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 深夜までアルバイトをしています。
examplePolite.english: I work part-time until late at night.

items.use: Roughly 4 to 7 p.m., while it gets dark; after that it's yoru.

example.ja: 夕方ごろ着くと思う。
example.english: I think I'll get there around early evening.

examplePolite.romaji: yuugata goro tsuku to omoimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 夕方ごろ着くと思います。
examplePolite.english: I expect to arrive in the early evening.

example.romaji: hiruma wa atsui kedo yoru wa suzushii.
example.ja: 昼間は暑いけど夜は涼しい。
example.english: It's hot in the day but cool at night.

examplePolite.romaji: hiruma wa atsui desu ga, yoru wa suzushii desu.
examplePolite.ja: 昼間は暑いですが、夜は涼しいです。
examplePolite.english: It's hot during the day, but cool at night.

items.notes: Hiru alone usually means noon or lunch; hiruma is the whole daylight stretch.

blocks.label: The four seasons
blocks.rationale: Name the seasons and say which one you like.
blocks.interference: None.

example.romaji: haru ni nattara hanami ikou yo.
example.ja: 春になったら花見行こうよ。
example.english: Let's go see the cherry blossoms when spring comes.

examplePolite.romaji: haru ni nattara hanami ni ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 春になったら花見に行きましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's go see the cherry blossoms when spring comes.

example.romaji: natsu wa yappari umi da ne.
example.ja: 夏はやっぱり海だね。
example.english: Summer just means the beach, doesn't it.

examplePolite.romaji: natsu wa yappari umi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 夏はやっぱり海ですね。
examplePolite.english: Summer really means the beach, doesn't it.

items.notes: natsuyasumi = the summer holidays.

example.ja: すっかり秋だね。
example.english: It's really autumn now.

examplePolite.romaji: sukkari aki desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: すっかり秋ですね。
examplePolite.english: It's really autumn now, isn't it.

example.ja: 今年の冬、寒いね。
example.english: This winter's cold, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: kotoshi no fuyu wa samui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今年の冬は寒いですね。
examplePolite.english: This winter is cold, isn't it.

items.use: kono kisetsu = this time of year.

example.ja: どの季節が一番好き？
example.english: Which season do you like best?

examplePolite.romaji: dono kisetsu ga ichiban suki desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どの季節が一番好きですか？
examplePolite.english: Which season do you like best?

blocks.label: Basic weather words
blocks.rationale: Say what the weather is like today or tomorrow.
blocks.interference: ame 'rain' sounds like ame 'candy'; hare is the noun, hareru the verb.

items.use: Rain falls with furu: ame ga furu.

example.romaji: ame furisou da kara, kasa motte ikou.
example.ja: 雨降りそうだから、傘持って行こう。
example.english: Looks like rain, so let's take an umbrella.

examplePolite.romaji: ame ga furisou na node, kasa o motte ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 雨が降りそうなので、傘を持って行きましょう。
examplePolite.english: It looks like rain, so let's take an umbrella.

items.notes: Same sound as ame 'candy'; only the pitch differs.

example.romaji: kyou wa ii tenki da ne.
example.ja: 今日はいい天気だね。
example.english: Nice weather today, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa ii tenki desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はいい天気ですね。
examplePolite.english: It's nice weather today, isn't it.

items.notes: otenki is the softer form. tenki ni naru = it'll clear up.

example.ja: 明日雪降るかもよ。
example.english: It might snow tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa yuki ga furu kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: 明日は雪が降るかもしれません。
examplePolite.english: It may snow tomorrow.

items.use: The forecast word for sunny: ashita wa hare.

example.ja: 明日は晴れだって。
example.english: They say it'll be sunny tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa hare da sou desu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日は晴れだそうです。
examplePolite.english: I hear it'll be sunny tomorrow.

items.notes: The verb is hareru (to clear up).

example.ja: 今日はずっと曇りみたい。
example.english: Looks like it'll be cloudy all day.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa zutto kumori mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はずっと曇りみたいです。
examplePolite.english: It looks like it'll be cloudy all day.

items.notes: kumo is a cloud. The verb kumoru gives kumotte kita, 'it's clouding over'.

example.ja: 明日の天気予報見た？
example.english: Did you see tomorrow's forecast?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no tenki yohou o mimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日の天気予報を見ましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you see tomorrow's weather forecast?

items.notes: Often just yohou: yohou da to ame da tte = the forecast says rain.

blocks.label: Rain starting and stopping
blocks.rationale: Say it's raining, it's stopped, or it's cleared up.
blocks.interference: yamu (weather stops by itself) gets mixed up with yameru (someone quits).

items.use: Only for things falling from the sky: ame ga furu, yuki ga furu.

example.ja: 外、雨まだ降ってる？
example.english: Is it still raining outside?

examplePolite.romaji: soto wa mada ame ga futte imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 外はまだ雨が降っていますか？
examplePolite.english: Is it still raining outside?

items.notes: Same sound as furu 'wave; dump someone'.

items.use: For weather or noise stopping by itself.

example.ja: 雨止んだから、行こうか。
example.english: The rain's stopped, so shall we go?

examplePolite.romaji: ame ga yanda node, ikimashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: 雨が止んだので、行きましょうか。
examplePolite.english: The rain has stopped, so shall we go?

items.notes: Not yameru (quit), which someone does on purpose.

items.use: Mostly past or -te form: hareta (it cleared up), hareteru (it's sunny).

example.ja: やっと晴れたね、よかった。
example.english: It finally cleared up, thank goodness.

examplePolite.romaji: yatto haremashita ne, yokatta desu.
examplePolite.ja: やっと晴れましたね、よかったです。
examplePolite.english: It's finally cleared up, I'm glad.

items.notes: The noun hare is the forecast word for 'sunny'.

blocks.label: How the air feels
blocks.rationale: Comment on warm days, cool evenings and muggy summers.
blocks.interference: atatakai (pleasant) vs atsui (too hot); suzushii (cool air) vs tsumetai (cold to the touch).

items.use: Pleasant warmth: weather, rooms, food, kind people. Unpleasant heat is atsui.

example.ja: 今日は暖かいね。
example.english: It's warm today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa atatakai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は暖かいですね。
examplePolite.english: It's warm today, isn't it.

items.notes: Casually said attakai. Written 温かい for food, drinks and kindness.

items.use: For air and weather; cold food or drinks are tsumetai.

example.ja: 夕方は涼しくなったね。
example.english: It's got cooler in the evenings.

examplePolite.romaji: yuugata wa suzushiku narimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 夕方は涼しくなりましたね。
examplePolite.english: It's become cooler in the evenings, hasn't it.

items.notes: suzushii is nice; samui is unpleasantly cold.

items.use: The standard complaint about Japanese summers.

example.ja: 今日、ほんとに蒸し暑いね。
example.english: It's so muggy today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hontou ni mushiatsui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は本当に蒸し暑いですね。
examplePolite.english: It's really muggy today, isn't it.

items.use: Comes up with hair, laundry and mould as much as weather.

example.romaji: kyou, shikke sugokute kami ga yabai.
example.ja: 今日、湿気すごくて髪がやばい。
example.english: It's so humid today, my hair's a mess.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa shikke ga sugokute, kami ga taihen desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は湿気がすごくて、髪が大変です。
examplePolite.english: It's so humid today, my hair is a disaster.

items.notes: Also read shikki.

blocks.label: Colour and four basics
blocks.rationale: Ask what colour something is and call it red, white, black or blue.
blocks.interference: aoi also covers green traffic lights, but grass is midori.

items.use: nani iro? asks what colour something is.

example.romaji: kuruma, nani iro ni shita no?
example.ja: 車、何色にしたの？
example.english: What colour did you go with for the car?

examplePolite.romaji: kuruma wa nani iro ni shimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 車は何色にしましたか？
examplePolite.english: What colour did you choose for the car?

items.notes: kiiro, chairo and haiiro all end in this word.

items.use: Adjective form, before a noun: akai kuruma.

example.ja: あの赤いかばん、かわいいね。
example.english: That red bag is cute.

examplePolite.romaji: ano akai kaban, kawaii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの赤いかばん、かわいいですね。
examplePolite.english: That red bag is cute, isn't it.

items.notes: kao ga akai = your face is red (embarrassed or drunk).
