example.ja: 新しい白いシャツ、もう汚れちゃった。
example.english: I already got my new white shirt dirty.

examplePolite.romaji: atarashii shiroi shatsu ga mou yogorete shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 新しい白いシャツがもう汚れてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: My new white shirt has already got dirty.

items.notes: Also 'pale' for skin: hada ga shiroi.

example.ja: 黒い靴しか持ってない。
example.english: I only own black shoes.

examplePolite.romaji: kuroi kutsu shika motte imasen.
examplePolite.ja: 黒い靴しか持っていません。
examplePolite.english: I only own black shoes.

items.notes: Also 'tanned': hi ni yakete kuroi.

items.use: Also covers green traffic lights and fresh greenery.

example.romaji: kyou, sora ga sugoku aoi ne.
example.ja: 今日、空がすごく青いね。
example.english: The sky's so blue today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa sora ga totemo aoi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は空がとても青いですね。
examplePolite.english: The sky is very blue today, isn't it.

items.notes: kaoiro ga aoi = you look pale.

blocks.label: Basic colours as nouns
blocks.rationale: Name a colour on its own: aka ga suki, kuro no fuku, the light's ao.
blocks.interference: akai before a noun vs aka on its own; the -i drops when the colour stands alone.

items.use: Noun form: aka ga suki, aka no kuruma. At lights, aka = red.

example.ja: 信号、赤だよ。止まって。
example.english: The light's red. Stop.

examplePolite.romaji: shingou ga aka desu yo. tomatte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 信号が赤ですよ。止まってください。
examplePolite.english: The light is red. Please stop.

items.use: Noun form: shiro ga ii, shiro no kuruma.

example.romaji: shiro to kuro, dotchi ga ii?
example.ja: 白と黒、どっちがいい？
example.english: White or black, which do you prefer?

examplePolite.romaji: shiro to kuro, dochira ga ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 白と黒、どちらがいいですか？
examplePolite.english: White or black, which would you prefer?

items.notes: Same sound as shiro 'castle'.

items.use: Noun form: kuro ga suki, kuro no fuku.

example.ja: いつも黒ばっかり着てるね。
example.english: You're always wearing black.

examplePolite.romaji: itsumo kuro bakari kite imasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: いつも黒ばかり着ていますね。
examplePolite.english: You always wear black, don't you.

items.use: Noun form. At lights, ao = green.

example.ja: 青になったよ、行こう。
example.english: It's turned green, let's go.

examplePolite.romaji: ao ni narimashita yo. ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 青になりましたよ。行きましょう。
examplePolite.english: It's turned green. Let's go.

items.notes: For clearly green things like grass or a shirt, say midori.

blocks.label: Green, yellow, pink, brown
blocks.rationale: Describe things in the next most common colours.
blocks.interference: midori (green things) vs ao (green traffic lights).

items.use: For green things and plants; traffic lights are ao.

example.romaji: midori ga ooi machi da ne.
example.ja: 緑が多い町だね。
example.english: This town has lots of green.

examplePolite.romaji: midori ga ooi machi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 緑が多い町ですね。
examplePolite.english: It's a town with a lot of greenery, isn't it.

items.use: kiiroi is the adjective before a noun: kiiroi kuruma.

example.ja: 黄色のセーター、似合うね。
example.english: The yellow sweater suits you.

examplePolite.romaji: kiiro no seetaa, niaimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 黄色のセーター、似合いますね。
examplePolite.english: The yellow sweater suits you.

example.romaji: kami, pinku ni someta n da.
example.ja: 髪、ピンクに染めたんだ。
example.english: I dyed my hair pink.

examplePolite.romaji: kami o pinku ni somemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 髪をピンクに染めました。
examplePolite.english: I dyed my hair pink.

items.notes: momoiro is the older native word for pink.

items.use: Literally 'tea colour'; chairoi is the adjective.

example.romaji: chairo no kutsu, doko de katta no?
example.ja: 茶色の靴、どこで買ったの？
example.english: Where'd you get the brown shoes?

examplePolite.romaji: chairo no kutsu, doko de kaimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 茶色の靴、どこで買いましたか？
examplePolite.english: Where did you buy the brown shoes?

blocks.label: Husband and wife
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about your spouse and ask about someone else's.
blocks.interference: tsuma and otto are your own spouse; okusan and goshujin are someone else's.

items.use: Someone else's wife; also a way to address a married woman.

example.ja: 奥さんは元気にしてる？
example.english: How's your wife doing?

examplePolite.romaji: okusan mo issho ni dou desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 奥さんも一緒にどうですか？
examplePolite.english: Why not bring your wife along too?

items.notes: Some men also say uchi no okusan for their own wife in casual talk.

items.use: Neutral word for your own wife; someone else's is okusan.

example.romaji: tsuma ga ninshin shita n da
example.ja: 妻が妊娠したんだ
example.english: My wife's pregnant.

examplePolite.romaji: tsuma to futari de sunde imasu
examplePolite.ja: 妻と二人で住んでいます
examplePolite.english: I live with my wife, just the two of us.

items.notes: In casual talk many men say yome instead.

items.use: Neutral word for your own husband; someone else's is goshujin.

example.ja: 夫が料理してくれる
example.english: My husband does the cooking.

examplePolite.romaji: otto wa kaishain desu
examplePolite.ja: 夫は会社員です
examplePolite.english: My husband is an office worker.

items.notes: In casual talk many women say danna instead.

items.use: Polite word for someone else's husband.

example.romaji: goshujin, nan no shigoto shiteru no?
example.ja: ご主人、何の仕事してるの？
example.english: What does your husband do?

examplePolite.romaji: goshujin wa ogenki desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ご主人はお元気ですか？
examplePolite.english: How is your husband?

items.notes: Also the master or owner of a shop or house.

blocks.label: Sons and daughters
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about your children and ask about other people's.
blocks.interference: Plain musuko and musume are your own; add -san for someone else's.

items.use: Your own daughter; someone else's is musumesan.

example.ja: 娘と買い物に行った
example.english: I went shopping with my daughter.

examplePolite.romaji: musume ga futari imasu
examplePolite.ja: 娘が二人います
examplePolite.english: I have two daughters.

items.use: Your own son; someone else's is musukosan.

example.ja: 息子が大学に入った
example.english: My son got into university.

examplePolite.romaji: musuko wa shougakusei desu
examplePolite.ja: 息子は小学生です
examplePolite.english: My son is in primary school.

items.use: Someone else's daughter.

example.ja: 娘さん、本当にかわいいね
example.english: Your daughter's really cute.

examplePolite.romaji: musumesan, hontou ni kawaii desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 娘さん、本当にかわいいですね
examplePolite.english: Your daughter is really cute.

items.use: Someone else's son.

example.ja: 息子さん、大きくなったね
example.english: Your son's grown so much.

examplePolite.romaji: musukosan, ookiku narimashita ne
examplePolite.ja: 息子さん、大きくなりましたね
examplePolite.english: Your son has grown so much.

items.use: Polite word for someone else's child or children; your own is kodomo.

example.ja: お子さん、いくつになった？
example.english: How old is your kid now?

examplePolite.romaji: okosan wa nannin desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お子さんは何人ですか？
examplePolite.english: How many children do you have?

blocks.label: Grandparents
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk to and about grandparents and elderly people.
blocks.interference: ojiisan and obaasan (grandparents) differ from ojisan and obasan (uncle, aunt) only by the long vowel.

items.use: Your own grandpa at home and with friends; also a friendly word for any old man.

example.ja: おじいちゃんの家に行く
example.english: I'm going to Grandpa's.

examplePolite.romaji: ojiichan to issho ni sunde imasu
examplePolite.ja: おじいちゃんと一緒に住んでいます
examplePolite.english: I live with my grandpa.

items.notes: In polite talk about your own grandfather, sofu is safer.

items.use: Your own grandma at home and with friends; also a friendly word for any old woman.

example.ja: おばあちゃんの料理、おいしいよ
example.english: Grandma's cooking is delicious.

examplePolite.romaji: obaachan wa inaka ni sunde imasu
examplePolite.ja: おばあちゃんは田舎に住んでいます
examplePolite.english: My grandma lives in the countryside.

items.notes: In polite talk about your own grandmother, sobo is safer.

items.use: Someone else's grandfather, or a polite word for an elderly man.

example.romaji: ano ojiisan, mainichi koko ni iru ne
example.ja: あのおじいさん、毎日ここにいるね
example.english: That old man is here every day.

examplePolite.romaji: ojiisan wa ogenki desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: おじいさんはお元気ですか？
examplePolite.english: How is your grandfather?

items.notes: Don't confuse with ojisan (uncle; middle-aged man): the long ii makes it grandfather.

items.use: Someone else's grandmother, or a polite word for an elderly woman.

example.ja: おばあさんに道聞かれた
example.english: An old lady asked me for directions.

examplePolite.romaji: obaasan ni michi o kikaremashita
examplePolite.ja: おばあさんに道を聞かれました
examplePolite.english: An old lady asked me for directions.

items.notes: Don't confuse with obasan (aunt; middle-aged woman): the long aa makes it grandmother.

items.use: Plain, homely word for your own grandpa, common with boys and men.

example.romaji: jiichan, mata tsuri ni ikou yo
example.ja: じいちゃん、また釣りに行こうよ
example.english: Grandpa, let's go fishing again.

items.use: Plain, homely word for your own grandma, common with boys and men.

example.ja: ばあちゃんの家、懐かしいな
example.english: Grandma's house brings back memories.

blocks.label: Mum and dad at home
blocks.rationale: Lets you call your parents the way families do at home.
blocks.interference: With outsiders adults switch to chichi and haha.

items.use: What many kids, and some adults, call their father at home.

example.ja: パパ、ちょっとこれ見て！
example.english: Dad, look at this!

items.notes: Adults talking to outsiders switch to chichi.

items.use: What many kids, and some adults, call their mother at home.

example.ja: ママ、これ買ってよ
example.english: Mum, buy me this!

items.notes: Also the woman who runs a bar or snack bar.

items.use: A more grown-up way to call your mother at home; common with teens and in dramas.

example.ja: 母さん、ちょっとコンビニ行ってくる
example.english: Mum, I'm just popping to the shop.

items.use: A more grown-up way to call your father at home; common with teens and in dramas.

example.romaji: tousan, chotto hanashi ga aru n da
example.ja: 父さん、ちょっと話があるんだ
example.english: Dad, I need to talk to you.

blocks.label: Calling siblings at home
blocks.rationale: Lets you call your older siblings the way families do.
blocks.interference: niichan and neechan also hail strangers and can sound rough.

items.use: What younger siblings call an older brother at home; also a friendly call to a young man.

example.ja: お兄ちゃん、ちょっと待ってよ！
example.english: Wait for me, big brother!

items.use: What younger siblings call an older sister at home; also a friendly call to a young woman.

example.ja: お姉ちゃん、この服借りていい？
example.english: Sis, can I borrow these clothes?

items.use: Shorter, rougher oniichan; older people also use it to hail a young man.

example.ja: 兄ちゃん、一緒に遊ぼう
example.english: Bro, come play with me.

items.use: Shorter, rougher oneechan; used to hail a young woman, it can sound crude.

example.ja: また姉ちゃんに怒られた
example.english: My big sister told me off again.

items.use: A grown-up, slightly formal way to call your older brother; common in dramas.

example.ja: 兄さん、久しぶりだね
example.english: Long time no see, brother.

examplePolite.romaji: niisan, ohisashiburi desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 兄さん、お久しぶりですね
examplePolite.english: It's been a long time, brother.

items.use: A grown-up, slightly formal way to call your older sister; common in dramas.

example.romaji: neesan, chotto soudan ga aru n da kedo
example.ja: 姉さん、ちょっと相談があるんだけど
example.english: Sis, can I ask your advice about something?

examplePolite.romaji: neesan, chotto soudan ga aru n desu ga
examplePolite.ja: 姉さん、ちょっと相談があるんですが
examplePolite.english: Sister, could I ask your advice about something?

blocks.label: Uncles, aunts and relatives
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about the wider family.
blocks.interference: ojisan and obasan also mean any middle-aged man or woman; mind the short vowel.

items.use: Any uncle, or any man around 40 to 60; kids use it for adult men.

example.ja: おじさんにお年玉もらった
example.english: I got New Year's money from my uncle.

examplePolite.romaji: ojisan ni otoshidama o moraimashita
examplePolite.ja: おじさんにお年玉をもらいました
examplePolite.english: I got New Year's money from my uncle.

items.notes: Calling a man ojisan can sting. Not ojiisan (grandfather).

items.use: Any aunt, or any woman around 40 to 60; kids use it for adult women.

example.ja: おばさんの家に泊まる
example.english: I'm staying at my aunt's.

examplePolite.romaji: obasan no ie ni tomarimasu
examplePolite.ja: おばさんの家に泊まります
examplePolite.english: I'm staying at my aunt's.

items.notes: Calling a woman obasan can offend. Not obaasan (grandmother).

items.use: Warmer, casual obasan; also how people call a friendly older woman at a shop.

example.ja: 食堂のおばちゃん、優しいよ
example.english: The canteen lady is really kind.

example.ja: 正月は親戚が集まる
example.english: Relatives all get together at New Year.

examplePolite.romaji: shinseki no kekkonshiki ni ikimasu
examplePolite.ja: 親戚の結婚式に行きます
examplePolite.english: I'm going to a relative's wedding.

example.romaji: itoko to onaji gakkou nan da
example.ja: いとこと同じ学校なんだ
example.english: My cousin goes to my school.

examplePolite.romaji: itoko to onaji gakkou ni kayotte imasu
examplePolite.ja: いとこと同じ学校に通っています
examplePolite.english: My cousin and I go to the same school.

blocks.label: Teeth, throat and lips
blocks.rationale: Lets you describe toothache, sore throats and dry lips.
blocks.interference: shita (tongue) sounds like shita (below); ha (tooth) like ha (leaf).

example.ja: 歯が痛くて寝れない
example.english: My tooth hurts so much I can't sleep.

examplePolite.romaji: ha ga itakute nemuremasen
examplePolite.ja: 歯が痛くて眠れません
examplePolite.english: My tooth hurts so much I can't sleep.

items.notes: Ha o migaku means brush your teeth; the dentist is haisha.

example.ja: 喉渇いた、なんか飲もう
example.english: I'm thirsty, let's get a drink.

examplePolite.romaji: nodo ga kawakimashita ne
examplePolite.ja: 喉が渇きましたね
examplePolite.english: I'm getting thirsty.

items.notes: Nodo ga kawaku means to be thirsty; nodo ga itai means a sore throat.

example.romaji: fuyu wa kuchibiru ga kasakasa ni naru
example.ja: 冬は唇がカサカサになる
example.english: My lips get really dry in winter.

examplePolite.romaji: fuyu wa kuchibiru ga kasakasa ni narimasu
examplePolite.ja: 冬は唇がカサカサになります
examplePolite.english: My lips get really dry in winter.

example.ja: 熱くて舌やけどした
example.english: It was so hot I burnt my tongue.

examplePolite.romaji: atsukute shita o yakedo shimashita
examplePolite.ja: 熱くて舌をやけどしました
examplePolite.english: It was so hot I burnt my tongue.

items.notes: Same sound as shita (below; under).

blocks.label: Lower back and legs
blocks.rationale: Lets you describe back pain and leg injuries.
blocks.interference: koshi is the lower back, not the whole back (senaka).

example.ja: 荷物持ち上げて腰痛めた
example.english: I hurt my back lifting the bags.

examplePolite.romaji: nimotsu o mochiagete koshi o itamemashita
examplePolite.ja: 荷物を持ち上げて腰を痛めました
examplePolite.english: I hurt my back lifting the bags.

items.notes: Back pain is usually koshi, not senaka.

example.ja: 転んで膝を擦りむいちゃった
example.english: I fell and scraped my knee.

examplePolite.romaji: koronde hiza o surimukimashita
examplePolite.ja: 転んで膝を擦りむきました
examplePolite.english: I fell and scraped my knee.

items.notes: Hiza no ue means on your lap.

items.use: The everyday word; shiri alone is cruder.

example.ja: ずっと座ってたからお尻痛い
example.english: My bum hurts from sitting all day.

examplePolite.romaji: zutto suwatte ita node oshiri ga itai desu
examplePolite.ja: ずっと座っていたのでお尻が痛いです
examplePolite.english: My bottom hurts from sitting all day.

blocks.label: Street directions
blocks.rationale: Give and follow directions: right, left, straight on, at the corner.
blocks.interference: migi and hidari get swapped under pressure.

example.ja: そこ、右に曲がって。
example.english: Turn right there.

examplePolite.romaji: soko o migi ni magatte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: そこを右に曲がってください。
examplePolite.english: Please turn right there.

items.notes: migigawa = the right-hand side.

example.romaji: hidari no hou ga chikai yo.
example.ja: 左の方が近いよ。
example.english: Going left is quicker.

examplePolite.romaji: hidari no hou ga chikai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 左の方が近いですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's closer if you go left.

items.notes: hidarikiki = left-handed.

items.use: Also 'directly': massugu kaeru = go straight home.

example.ja: この道、まっすぐ行って。
example.english: Go straight along this road.

examplePolite.romaji: kono michi o massugu itte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: この道をまっすぐ行ってください。
examplePolite.english: Please go straight along this road.

items.notes: massugu na hito = an honest, straightforward person.

items.use: The outside corner you turn at; a room's inside corner is sumi.

example.romaji: ano kado no konbini de matteru ne.
example.ja: あの角のコンビニで待ってるね。
example.english: I'll wait at the convenience store on that corner.

examplePolite.romaji: ano kado no konbini de matte imasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの角のコンビニで待っていますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll be waiting at the convenience store on that corner.

blocks.label: Next to and near
blocks.rationale: Say where something is: next to, near, beside, between.
blocks.interference: tonari is next to the same kind of thing; yoko is beside anything; soba is just near.

items.use: Right beside, usually the same kind of thing: seats, houses, people.

example.ja: 隣、座ってもいい？
example.english: Mind if I sit next to you?

examplePolite.romaji: tonari ni suwatte mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 隣に座ってもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: May I sit next to you?

items.notes: tonari no hito = the neighbour, or the person in the next seat.

items.use: Close by, vaguer than tonari or yoko: eki no soba = near the station.

example.romaji: eki no soba ni sunderu n da.
example.ja: 駅のそばに住んでるんだ。
example.english: I live near the station.

examplePolite.romaji: eki no soba ni sunde imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 駅のそばに住んでいます。
examplePolite.english: I live near the station.

items.notes: Same sound as soba noodles.

items.use: Beside anything at all, not just the same kind of thing.

example.romaji: kagi, terebi no yoko ni oita yo.
example.ja: 鍵、テレビの横に置いたよ。
example.english: I put the keys next to the TV.

examplePolite.romaji: kagi wa terebi no yoko ni okimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 鍵はテレビの横に置きました。
examplePolite.english: I put the keys next to the TV.

items.notes: yoko ni naru = lie down.

items.use: X to Y no aida = between X and Y.

example.romaji: ginkou to yuubinkyoku no aida ni aru yo.
example.ja: 銀行と郵便局の間にあるよ。
example.english: It's between the bank and the post office.

examplePolite.romaji: ginkou to yuubinkyoku no aida ni arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 銀行と郵便局の間にあります。
examplePolite.english: It's between the bank and the post office.

items.notes: kono aida = the other day.

blocks.label: Around here and there
blocks.rationale: Point to a rough area near you, near them or away from both, and ask whereabouts.
blocks.interference: sono hen (near you) vs ano hen (away from both of us).

example.ja: この辺にコンビニある？
example.english: Is there a convenience store around here?

examplePolite.romaji: kono hen ni konbini wa arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: この辺にコンビニはありますか？
examplePolite.english: Is there a convenience store around here?

items.notes: Also 'stop here': kyou wa kono hen de = let's call it a day.

items.use: Near the listener, or just 'somewhere around there'.

example.ja: かばん、その辺に置いといて。
example.english: Just leave your bag around there.

examplePolite.romaji: kaban wa sono hen ni oite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: かばんはその辺に置いてください。
examplePolite.english: Please put your bag over there.

items.notes: Also 'that part': sono hen wa daijoubu = that part's fine.

items.use: An area away from you both, or one you both know.

example.romaji: mukashi, ano hen ni sundeta n da.
example.ja: 昔、あの辺に住んでたんだ。
example.english: I used to live around there.

examplePolite.romaji: mukashi, ano hen ni sunde imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昔、あの辺に住んでいました。
examplePolite.english: I used to live around there.

items.use: Softer than doko when you only want a rough area.

example.ja: どの辺に住んでるの？
example.english: Whereabouts do you live?

examplePolite.romaji: dono hen ni sunde imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どの辺に住んでいますか？
examplePolite.english: Whereabouts do you live?

items.notes: Also 'which part?': dono hen ga yokatta? = which part did you like?

items.use: Vague: sokora ni aru = it's around there somewhere.

example.ja: 眼鏡？そこらにない？
example.english: Your glasses? Aren't they around there somewhere?

items.notes: Also 'or so': ichiman en ka sokora = ten thousand yen or so.

blocks.label: Blunt you
blocks.rationale: Lets you recognise rough ways of saying you.
blocks.interference: omae is friendly among male friends but aggressive from strangers.

items.use: Men use it with close friends or to talk down; from a stranger it's aggressive.

example.romaji: omae, nani shiteru n da yo
example.ja: お前、何してるんだよ
example.english: What the hell are you doing?

items.notes: In polite talk, use the person's name with -san.

items.use: Short for anata; blunt or familiar, common with older women and in arguments.

example.romaji: anta ni wa kankei nai desho
example.ja: あんたには関係ないでしょ
example.english: That's none of your business.

items.use: Rough 'you' for a group; common among male friends and from coaches.

example.ja: お前ら、ちょっとうるさいぞ
example.english: You lot, keep it down.

items.notes: Polite talk uses minasan for 'you all'.

blocks.label: That guy, those guys
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk casually about people who aren't here.
blocks.interference: koitsu, soitsu and aitsu follow the same near, middle and far split as kore, sore and are.

items.use: Casual word for a person or a thing: ii yatsu is a good guy, akai yatsu is the red one.

example.ja: 彼、いいやつだよ
example.english: He's a good guy.

items.notes: In polite talk, say hito for people and mono or no for things.

items.use: Casual 'him' or 'her' for someone not here; friendly or dismissive by tone.

example.ja: あいつ、また遅刻だよ
example.english: He's late again.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa mata chikoku desu
examplePolite.ja: あの人はまた遅刻です
examplePolite.english: He's late again.

items.use: Rough 'this person' for someone right beside you.

example.ja: こいつ、俺の友達
example.english: This guy's my friend.

examplePolite.romaji: kono hito wa watashi no tomodachi desu
examplePolite.ja: この人は私の友達です
examplePolite.english: This is my friend.

items.notes: Also for things and pets: koitsu can mean this thing.

items.use: Rough word for someone the other person just brought up.

example.ja: そいつ、ムカつくやつだな
example.english: That guy sounds like a jerk.

examplePolite.romaji: sono hito wa iya na hito desu ne
examplePolite.ja: その人は嫌な人ですね
examplePolite.english: That person sounds unpleasant.

example.ja: あいつら、まだ来ないの？
example.english: Those guys still aren't here?

examplePolite.romaji: ano hitotachi wa mada kimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの人たちはまだ来ませんか？
examplePolite.english: Aren't they here yet?

items.use: Rough 'them', often for rivals or enemies.

example.romaji: yatsura ni makeru wake ni wa ikanai
example.ja: やつらに負けるわけにはいかない
example.english: No way we're losing to those guys.

blocks.label: We with -ra
blocks.rationale: Lets you make casual plurals and hear the we-words in songs.
blocks.interference: -ra sounds rougher than -tachi; bokura is softer than orera.

items.use: Added to pronouns and names for 'and the others': karera, bokura, tanaka-ra.

example.ja: 彼らも来るって
example.english: They said they're coming too.

examplePolite.romaji: karera mo kuru sou desu
examplePolite.ja: 彼らも来るそうです
examplePolite.english: I hear they're coming too.

items.notes: Rougher than -tachi on most words; karera (they) is neutral.

items.use: Casual male 'we', softer than orera; very common in songs.

example.ja: 僕ら、もう大人だよ
example.english: We're grown-ups now.

examplePolite.romaji: bokura wa mou otona desu
examplePolite.ja: 僕らはもう大人です
examplePolite.english: We're adults now.

example.ja: 俺らでなんとかしようぜ
example.english: Let's sort it out ourselves.

examplePolite.romaji: watashitachi de nantoka shimashou
examplePolite.ja: 私たちでなんとかしましょう
examplePolite.english: Let's sort it out ourselves.

items.use: Young women's and western Japan's casual 'we'.

example.romaji: uchira, zutto tomodachi da yo ne
example.ja: うちら、ずっと友達だよね
example.english: We'll always be friends, right?

blocks.label: Common country names
blocks.rationale: Say where you and other people are from.
blocks.interference: igirisu (the UK) isn't guessable from 'England'.

items.use: The everyday name for the US; beikoku is the news word.

example.ja: アメリカに住んでたことある。
example.english: I've lived in America before.

examplePolite.romaji: amerika ni sunde ita koto ga arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: アメリカに住んでいたことがあります。
examplePolite.english: I have lived in America before.

example.romaji: raigetsu, chuugoku ni shutchou nan da.
example.ja: 来月、中国に出張なんだ。
example.english: I've got a work trip to China next month.

examplePolite.romaji: raigetsu, chuugoku ni shutchou ni ikimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 来月、中国に出張に行きます。
examplePolite.english: I'm going to China on business next month.

items.notes: Chinese food is chuuka. Also the name of a region of western Japan.

items.use: Means South Korea; North Korea is kitachousen.

example.ja: 韓国旅行、どうだった？
example.english: How was your trip to Korea?

examplePolite.romaji: kankoku ryokou wa dou deshita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 韓国旅行はどうでしたか？
examplePolite.english: How was your trip to Korea?

items.use: Covers the UK and England alike; British people are igirisujin.

example.romaji: igirisu tte, ame ooi n desho?
example.ja: イギリスって、雨多いんでしょ？
example.english: Britain gets a lot of rain, right?

examplePolite.romaji: igirisu wa ame ga ooi n desu yo ne?
examplePolite.ja: イギリスは雨が多いんですよね？
examplePolite.english: It rains a lot in Britain, doesn't it?

items.notes: Not guessable from 'England'; eikoku is the news word.

example.ja: オーストラリアから来たんだ。
example.english: I'm from Australia.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa oosutoraria kara kimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 私はオーストラリアから来ました。
examplePolite.english: I'm from Australia.

blocks.label: Home and abroad
blocks.rationale: Talk about home countries, foreigners and travel abroad.
blocks.interference: kaigai (going overseas) vs gaikoku (foreign countries themselves).

example.romaji: kuni ni wa itsu kaeru no?
example.ja: 国にはいつ帰るの？
example.english: When are you going back home?

examplePolite.romaji: kuni ni wa itsu kaeru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 国にはいつ帰るんですか？
examplePolite.english: When are you going back to your country?

items.notes: okuni wa dochira desu ka? is the polite 'where are you from?'

items.use: The usual word for going abroad: kaigai ryokou = a trip overseas.

example.ja: 海外旅行、行ったことある？
example.english: Have you ever been overseas?

examplePolite.romaji: kaigai ryokou ni itta koto wa arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 海外旅行に行ったことはありますか？
examplePolite.english: Have you ever travelled overseas?

items.notes: kaigai is about going abroad; gaikoku is the foreign countries themselves.

items.use: Any country that isn't Japan.

example.romaji: itsuka gaikoku ni sunde mitai na.
example.ja: いつか外国に住んでみたいな。
example.english: I'd like to live abroad someday.

examplePolite.romaji: itsuka gaikoku ni sunde mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: いつか外国に住んでみたいです。
examplePolite.english: I'd like to live abroad someday.

items.use: The neutral word for non-Japanese people.

example.ja: この辺、外国人多いね。
example.english: Lots of foreigners around here, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: kono hen wa gaikokujin ga ooi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この辺は外国人が多いですね。
examplePolite.english: There are a lot of foreigners around here.

items.notes: You'll also hear the clipped gaijin, which many find rude.

items.use: Mostly for travel and flights: kokunai ryokou, kokunaisen (domestic flights).

example.romaji: kotoshi wa kokunai ryokou ni shiyou ka.
example.ja: 今年は国内旅行にしようか。
example.english: Shall we travel within Japan this year?

examplePolite.romaji: kotoshi wa kokunai ryokou ni shimashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: 今年は国内旅行にしましょうか。
examplePolite.english: Shall we travel within the country this year?

items.notes: The usual contrast is kaigai (overseas).

blocks.label: Five basic tastes
blocks.rationale: Say whether food is sweet, spicy, bitter, sour or salty.
blocks.interference: karai means spicy, but in western Japan also salty; shoppai is the eastern word for salty.

items.use: Second sense: kodomo ni amai = soft on the kids.

example.ja: これ、ちょっと甘すぎるかも。
example.english: This might be a bit too sweet.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa chotto amasugiru kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: これはちょっと甘すぎるかもしれません。
examplePolite.english: This may be a little too sweet.

items.notes: amai mono = sweets; amai mono ga suki = I have a sweet tooth.

items.use: Chilli heat; hot in temperature is atsui.

example.ja: これ辛い？食べられるかな。
example.english: Is this spicy? Wonder if I can eat it.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa karai desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これは辛いですか？
examplePolite.english: Is this spicy?

items.notes: In western Japan it can also mean salty.

items.use: Also for experiences: nigai omoide = a bitter memory.

example.ja: このコーヒー、ちょっと苦すぎる。
example.english: This coffee is a bit too bitter.

examplePolite.romaji: kono koohii wa chotto nigasugimasu.
examplePolite.ja: このコーヒーはちょっと苦すぎます。
examplePolite.english: This coffee is a little too bitter.

items.notes: Don't confuse with nigate (bad at; not a fan of).

example.ja: このいちご、まだ酸っぱいね。
example.english: These strawberries are still sour.

examplePolite.romaji: kono ichigo wa mada suppai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: このいちごはまだ酸っぱいですね。
examplePolite.english: These strawberries are still sour, aren't they.

items.use: The everyday word for too salty, mainly in eastern Japan.

example.ja: このスープ、ちょっとしょっぱくない？
example.english: Isn't this soup a bit salty?

examplePolite.romaji: kono suupu, sukoshi shoppai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: このスープ、少ししょっぱいですね。
examplePolite.english: This soup is a little salty.

items.notes: Also slang for lame or disappointing.

blocks.label: Bad taste and texture
blocks.rationale: Say food tastes bad, is tough, or is tender.
blocks.interference: mazui also means 'uh-oh, that's bad', not just bad taste.

items.use: mazui! alone means 'uh-oh, this is bad'.

example.ja: このラーメン、ほんとにまずい。
example.english: This ramen is really bad.

examplePolite.romaji: kono raamen wa chotto mazui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: このラーメンはちょっとまずいですね。
examplePolite.english: This ramen isn't very good.

items.notes: Blunt about food someone made for you; say amari oishiku nai instead.

items.use: For food, beds and bodies; also stiff or formal (katai hanashi).

example.ja: この肉、ちょっと硬いね。
example.english: This meat's a bit tough.

examplePolite.romaji: kono niku wa sukoshi katai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この肉は少し硬いですね。
examplePolite.english: This meat is a little tough.

items.notes: atama ga katai = stubborn, set in their ways.

items.use: For food, cushions and skin; also a gentle manner.

example.ja: この肉、すごい柔らかい！
example.english: This meat is so tender!

examplePolite.romaji: kono niku wa totemo yawarakai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この肉はとても柔らかいですね。
examplePolite.english: This meat is very tender.

blocks.label: Animals, machines, books
blocks.rationale: Lets you count pets, cars and devices, and books.
blocks.interference: -hiki changes like -hon (ippiki, sanbiki, roppiki); -dai never changes.

items.english: small animals (counter): dogs, cats, fish, insects
items.use: Same changes as -hon: ippiki, nihiki, sanbiki, yonhiki, gohiki, roppiki, nanahiki, happiki, kyuuhiki, juppiki; how many is nanbiki.

example.romaji: uchi, neko ga nihiki iru n da.
example.ja: うち、猫が二匹いるんだ。
example.english: We've got two cats at home.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi ni wa neko ga nihiki imasu.
examplePolite.ja: うちには猫が二匹います。
examplePolite.english: We have two cats at home.

items.notes: Large animals like cows and horses take -tou instead.

items.english: machines and vehicles (counter): cars, bikes, phones, computers
items.use: No sound changes: ichidai, nidai, sandai ... juudai; how many is nandai.

example.ja: 車、二台あるの？
example.english: You have two cars?

examplePolite.romaji: kuruma ga nidai aru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 車が二台あるんですか？
examplePolite.english: You have two cars?

items.use: issatsu, nisatsu, sansatsu, yonsatsu, gosatsu, rokusatsu, nanasatsu, hassatsu, kyuusatsu, jussatsu; how many is nansatsu.

example.romaji: toshokan de hon sansatsu karita yo.
example.ja: 図書館で本三冊借りたよ。
example.english: I borrowed three books from the library.

examplePolite.romaji: toshokan de hon o sansatsu karimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 図書館で本を三冊借りました。
examplePolite.english: I borrowed three books from the library.

blocks.label: Turns, floors and rooms
blocks.rationale: Lets you name a turn, a floor, a place in line, a room or an address block.
blocks.interference: Floor -kai sounds like 'times' -kai; sangai is 3rd floor but sankai is three times.

items.use: After a number for numbered things like platforms and lines (sanban = number 3); dare no ban = whose turn.

example.ja: 次、誰の番？
example.english: Whose turn is it next?

examplePolite.romaji: tsugi wa dare no ban desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 次は誰の番ですか？
examplePolite.english: Whose turn is it next?

items.notes: No sound changes; which number is nanban. Ichiban also means 'most, best'.

items.use: ikkai, nikai, sangai, yonkai, gokai, rokkai, nanakai, hakkai, kyuukai, jukkai; which floor is nangai; basement 1 is chika ikkai.

example.ja: トイレは二階だよ。
example.english: The toilet's on the second floor.

examplePolite.romaji: toire wa nikai ni arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: トイレは二階にあります。
examplePolite.english: The toilet is on the second floor.

items.notes: Japan counts the ground floor as ikkai, so nikai is the British first floor. Sangai (3rd floor) voices; sankai (three times) does not.

items.use: ichibanme, nibanme, sanbanme ...; which one in order is nanbanme.

example.romaji: migi kara nibanme no hito, dare?
example.ja: 右から二番目の人、誰？
example.english: Who's the second person from the right?

examplePolite.romaji: migi kara nibanme no hito wa dare desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 右から二番目の人は誰ですか？
examplePolite.english: Who is the second person from the right?

items.notes: With native numbers, -me does the same job: futatsume = the second one.

items.use: After the number on a door: hotel rooms, flats, classrooms; which room is nangoushitsu.

example.ja: 部屋は二百一号室だよ。
example.english: The room is 201.

examplePolite.romaji: heya wa nihyakuichigoushitsu desu.
examplePolite.ja: 部屋は二百一号室です。
examplePolite.english: The room is 201.

items.notes: Room numbers are often read digit by digit with maru for zero: nimaruichi.

items.use: Comes after the district name: sanchoume; the changes are itchoume, hatchoume, jutchoume; which block is nanchoume.

example.romaji: uchi, sanchoume no kouen no chikaku da yo.
example.ja: うち、三丁目の公園の近くだよ。
example.english: My place is near the park in block 3.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi wa sanchoume no kouen no chikaku desu.
examplePolite.ja: うちは三丁目の公園の近くです。
examplePolite.english: My home is near the park in block 3.

items.notes: Mostly heard when giving or reading an address.

blocks.label: Units of measure
blocks.rationale: Lets you give distances, heights, weights and volumes.
blocks.interference: Kiro can be kilograms or kilometres; ikkiro and issenchi shrink like native counters.

items.use: Context says weight or distance; the number shortens before it: ikkiro, rokkiro, hakkiro, jukkiro, hyakkiro.

example.romaji: eki made gokiro gurai aru yo.
example.ja: 駅まで五キロぐらいあるよ。
example.english: It's about five kilometres to the station.

examplePolite.romaji: eki made gokiro gurai arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 駅まで五キロぐらいあります。
examplePolite.english: It's about five kilometres to the station.

items.notes: Speed is jisoku: jisoku hyakkiro = 100 km/h.

items.use: No sound changes: ichimeetoru, nimeetoru, hyakumeetoru; how far is nanmeetoru.

example.romaji: hyakumeetoru saki ni konbini aru yo.
example.ja: 百メートル先にコンビニあるよ。
example.english: There's a convenience store 100 metres ahead.

examplePolite.romaji: hyakumeetoru saki ni konbini ga arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 百メートル先にコンビニがあります。
examplePolite.english: There's a convenience store 100 metres ahead.

items.notes: Height is usually given in senchi, not meetoru.

items.use: Sound changes: issenchi, hassenchi, jussenchi; height is usually said in senchi.

example.ja: 前髪、五センチぐらい切って。
example.english: Cut my fringe by about five centimetres.

examplePolite.romaji: maegami o gosenchi gurai kitte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 前髪を五センチぐらい切ってください。
examplePolite.english: Please cut my fringe by about five centimetres.

items.notes: Short for senchimeetoru.

items.use: Common when buying meat or food by weight: hyakuguramu = 100 g.

example.ja: 豚肉、二百グラムでいい？
example.english: Is 200 grams of pork okay?

examplePolite.romaji: butaniku, nihyakuguramu de ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 豚肉、二百グラムでいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Is 200 grams of pork all right?

items.use: For drinks and bottle sizes: nirittoru no pettobotoru = a two-litre plastic bottle.

example.ja: 水、毎日二リットル飲んでるよ。
example.english: I drink two litres of water a day.

examplePolite.romaji: mizu o mainichi nirittoru nonde imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 水を毎日二リットル飲んでいます。
examplePolite.english: I drink two litres of water every day.

blocks.label: Set count expressions
blocks.rationale: Lets you say double, a few times, never once, and overnight.
blocks.interference: nibai (twice as much) vs nikai (twice); nandoka (a few times) vs nando mo (again and again).

items.use: Bai alone means double (bai ni naru = doubles); nibai, sanbai ... = two, three times as much.

example.romaji: nedan ga bai ni natta n da yo.
example.ja: 値段が倍になったんだよ。
example.english: The price doubled.

examplePolite.romaji: nedan ga bai ni natta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 値段が倍になったんです。
examplePolite.english: The price has doubled.

items.notes: Don't mix with -kai: nibai is twice as much, nikai is twice (two times).

items.use: A vague count like 'a couple of times'; casual speech also says nankai ka.

example.romaji: soko, nandoka itta koto aru yo.
example.ja: そこ、何度か行ったことあるよ。
example.english: I've been there a few times.

examplePolite.romaji: soko ni wa nandoka itta koto ga arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: そこには何度か行ったことがあります。
examplePolite.english: I've been there a few times.

items.notes: Not nando mo, which means 'again and again'.

items.use: Always with a negative verb: ichido mo nai = never.

example.romaji: sushi, ichido mo tabeta koto nai no?
example.ja: 寿司、一度も食べたことないの？
example.english: You've never had sushi, not even once?

examplePolite.romaji: sushi o ichido mo tabeta koto ga nai n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 寿司を一度も食べたことがないんですか？
examplePolite.english: You've never had sushi, not even once?

items.notes: Casual speech also says ikkai mo with the same meaning.

items.use: Hitobanjuu = all night long.

example.ja: 一晩寝れば治るよ。
example.english: A night's sleep will fix it.

examplePolite.romaji: hitoban nereba naorimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 一晩寝れば治りますよ。
examplePolite.english: A night's sleep will fix it.

items.notes: For hotel stays, count nights with -haku: ippaku, nihaku.

blocks.label: Comparing ages
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about age, being the same age, or someone's decade.
blocks.interference: nijuudai (in one's twenties) vs hatachi (exactly twenty).

items.use: The formal word, used on forms, in rules and in news; in conversation people mostly say toshi.

example.ja: 年齢関係ないよ。
example.english: Age doesn't matter.

examplePolite.romaji: nenrei wa kankei arimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 年齢は関係ありません。
examplePolite.english: Age doesn't matter.

items.use: Said of people born in the same year, a quick bond in Japan: onaidoshi da ne = we're the same age.

example.ja: えー、同い年なんだ！
example.english: Oh, we're the same age!

examplePolite.romaji: ee, onaidoshi nan desu ne!
examplePolite.ja: えー、同い年なんですね！
examplePolite.english: Oh, we're the same age!

items.notes: Older is toshiue, younger is toshishita.

items.use: Swap the number for any decade: sanjuudai = thirties, yonjuudai = forties.

example.ja: たぶん二十代後半かな。
example.english: Probably in their late twenties.

examplePolite.romaji: tabun nijuudai kouhan da to omoimasu.
examplePolite.ja: たぶん二十代後半だと思います。
examplePolite.english: I think they're in their late twenties.

items.notes: Zenhan = early, kouhan = late: sanjuudai zenhan = early thirties.

blocks.label: Years later and since
blocks.rationale: Lets you say a few years, years later, and the first time in years.
blocks.interference: -nengo (years later) vs -nenburi (first time in years).

items.english: for the first time in ... years
items.use: Often heard when meeting someone again: gonenburi = first time in five years.

example.romaji: kare ni au no, gonenburi da yo.
example.ja: 彼に会うの、五年ぶりだよ。
example.english: It's been five years since I last saw him.

examplePolite.romaji: kare ni au no wa gonenburi desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼に会うのは五年ぶりです。
examplePolite.english: It's been five years since I last saw him.

items.notes: -buri works with any span: mikkaburi, and hisashiburi = it's been a while.

items.use: sannengo = three years later or in three years' time; the opposite is -nen mae (years ago).

example.ja: 十年後、何してると思う？
example.english: What do you think you'll be doing in ten years?

examplePolite.romaji: juunengo, nani o shite iru to omoimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 十年後、何をしていると思いますか？
examplePolite.english: What do you think you'll be doing in ten years?

items.notes: The same -go works with other spans: mikkago = three days later.

items.use: Mostly in suunen mae (a few years ago) and suunengo (in a few years).

example.romaji: suunen mae ni hikkoshite kita n da.
example.ja: 数年前に引っ越してきたんだ。
example.english: I moved here a few years ago.

examplePolite.romaji: suunen mae ni hikkoshite kimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 数年前に引っ越してきました。
examplePolite.english: I moved here a few years ago.

blocks.label: Further back and ahead
blocks.rationale: Lets you go two weeks or two years either way, or a day either side of an event.
blocks.interference: Zenjitsu and yokujitsu count from an event, not from today.

example.ja: 先々週から風邪ひいてる。
example.english: I've had a cold since the week before last.

examplePolite.romaji: sensenshuu kara kaze o hiite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 先々週から風邪をひいています。
examplePolite.english: I've had a cold since the week before last.

items.notes: Sensen- means two back: sensengetsu is the month before last.

example.romaji: shiken wa saraishuu da kara, mada daijoubu.
example.ja: 試験は再来週だから、まだ大丈夫。
example.english: The exam's the week after next, so there's still time.

examplePolite.romaji: shiken wa saraishuu na node, mada daijoubu desu.
examplePolite.ja: 試験は再来週なので、まだ大丈夫です。
examplePolite.english: The exam is the week after next, so I still have time.

items.notes: Sarai- means two ahead: saraigetsu is the month after next.

example.ja: 一昨年結婚したんだ。
example.english: I got married the year before last.

examplePolite.romaji: ototoshi kekkon shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 一昨年結婚しました。
examplePolite.english: I got married the year before last.

items.notes: Don't mix with ototoi (the day before yesterday).

example.ja: 再来年卒業する予定。
example.english: I'm due to graduate the year after next.

examplePolite.romaji: sarainen sotsugyou suru yotei desu.
examplePolite.ja: 再来年卒業する予定です。
examplePolite.english: I'm due to graduate the year after next.

items.use: Counted from a set day, not from today; for 'yesterday' say kinou.

example.romaji: shiken no zenjitsu wa hayaku neta.
example.ja: 試験の前日は早く寝た。
example.english: I went to bed early the day before the exam.

examplePolite.romaji: shiken no zenjitsu wa hayaku nemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 試験の前日は早く寝ました。
examplePolite.english: I went to bed early the day before the exam.

items.notes: Mae no hi is the softer everyday phrase.

items.english: the next day; the following day
items.use: Counted from a set or past day, not from today; for 'tomorrow' say ashita.

example.romaji: nomikai no yokujitsu wa itsumo futsukayoi.
example.ja: 飲み会の翌日はいつも二日酔い。
example.english: I'm always hungover the day after a drinking party.

examplePolite.romaji: nomikai no yokujitsu wa itsumo futsukayoi desu.
examplePolite.ja: 飲み会の翌日はいつも二日酔いです。
examplePolite.english: I'm always hungover the day after a drinking party.

items.notes: Tsugi no hi is the everyday phrase.

blocks.label: Formal meal words
blocks.rationale: Lets you follow dinner and breakfast talk at hotels and on menus.
blocks.interference: Yuushoku (dinner) vs choushoku (breakfast).

items.use: Same as bangohan; common at home.

example.ja: 夕飯の支度しなきゃ。
example.english: I need to get dinner ready.

examplePolite.romaji: yuuhan no shitaku o shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 夕飯の支度をします。
examplePolite.english: I'll get dinner ready.

items.use: Heard at hotels, restaurants and in announcements; at home say bangohan or yuuhan.

example.romaji: yuushoku wa hoteru de taberu yo.
example.ja: 夕食はホテルで食べるよ。
example.english: We'll have dinner at the hotel.

examplePolite.romaji: yuushoku wa hoteru de tabemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 夕食はホテルで食べます。
examplePolite.english: We'll have dinner at the hotel.

items.use: Heard at hotels and on menus; at home say asagohan.

example.ja: 朝食って何時から？
example.english: What time does breakfast start?

examplePolite.romaji: choushoku wa nanji kara desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 朝食は何時からですか？
examplePolite.english: What time is breakfast served from?

items.notes: Lunch in the same style is chuushoku.

blocks.label: Wind and storms
blocks.rationale: Talk about wind, typhoons, thunder and the rainy season.
blocks.interference: kaze 'wind' and kaze 'a cold' sound the same.

items.use: Wind blows with fuku: kaze ga fuku. Windy is kaze ga tsuyoi.

example.romaji: kyou wa kaze ga tsuyoi ne.
example.ja: 今日は風が強いね。
example.english: It's really windy today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kaze ga tsuyoi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は風が強いですね。
examplePolite.english: It's windy today, isn't it.

items.notes: Same sound as kaze 'a cold' (kaze o hiku = catch a cold).

items.use: Typhoons come late summer to autumn; taifuu ga kuru = a typhoon is coming.

example.romaji: taifuu kuru kara, ashita yasumi kamo.
example.ja: 台風来るから、明日休みかも。
example.english: A typhoon's coming, so tomorrow might be a day off.

examplePolite.romaji: taifuu ga kuru node, ashita wa yasumi ni naru kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: 台風が来るので、明日は休みになるかもしれません。
examplePolite.english: A typhoon is coming, so tomorrow may be a day off.

items.use: One word for both; kaminari ga naru = it thunders.

example.ja: うわ、雷鳴ってる、怖い。
example.english: Whoa, it's thundering. Scary.

examplePolite.romaji: kaminari ga natte imasu ne. kowai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 雷が鳴っていますね。怖いです。
examplePolite.english: It's thundering, isn't it. It's scary.

items.notes: kaminari ga ochiru = lightning strikes.

items.use: Japan's early-summer rains, roughly June to mid-July.

example.romaji: mou tsuyu ni haitta n da.
example.ja: もう梅雨に入ったんだ。
example.english: So the rainy season's started already.

examplePolite.romaji: mou tsuyu ni hairimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: もう梅雨に入りましたね。
examplePolite.english: The rainy season has started already, hasn't it.

items.notes: tsuyuake = the end of the rainy season. Same sound as tsuyu 'dipping sauce'.

blocks.label: Purple, orange, grey
blocks.rationale: Round out the colours for clothes and the sky.
blocks.interference: haiiro and the loanword gurei both mean grey.

example.ja: 紫の傘、誰の？
example.english: Whose purple umbrella is this?

examplePolite.romaji: murasaki no kasa wa dare no desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 紫の傘は誰のですか？
examplePolite.english: Whose is the purple umbrella?

items.use: orenji iro makes it clear you mean the colour.

example.romaji: yuuhi, orenji iro de kirei da ne.
example.ja: 夕日、オレンジ色できれいだね。
example.english: The sunset's such a pretty orange.

examplePolite.romaji: yuuhi ga orenji iro de kirei desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 夕日がオレンジ色できれいですね。
examplePolite.english: The sunset is a beautiful orange, isn't it.

items.use: Literally 'ash colour'. For clothes, the loanword gurei is just as common.

example.romaji: kyou wa sora ga haiiro da ne.
example.ja: 今日は空が灰色だね。
example.english: The sky's grey today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa sora ga haiiro desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は空が灰色ですね。
examplePolite.english: The sky is grey today, isn't it.

blocks.label: Married couple words
blocks.rationale: Lets you understand the casual and older words couples use.
blocks.interference: shujin and danna are your own husband; goshujin and dannasan are someone else's.

items.use: Casual word for your own husband; someone else's is dannasan.

example.ja: 旦那、まだ帰ってこない
example.english: My husband still isn't home.

examplePolite.romaji: danna wa kyou shutchou desu
examplePolite.ja: 旦那は今日出張です
examplePolite.english: My husband's away on business today.

example.ja: あの二人、夫婦なの？
example.english: Are those two married?

examplePolite.romaji: fuufu de kissaten o yatte imasu
examplePolite.ja: 夫婦で喫茶店をやっています
examplePolite.english: My wife and I run a café together.

items.use: Older-style word a wife uses for her own husband, mostly in polite talk.

example.ja: 主人はまだ寝てる
example.english: My husband's still asleep.

examplePolite.romaji: shujin wa ima rusu desu
examplePolite.ja: 主人は今留守です
examplePolite.english: My husband is out right now.

items.notes: Also means master or owner. Some avoid it as old-fashioned.

items.use: Many men use it casually for their own wife; traditionally it means a son's wife.

example.ja: 昨日嫁に怒られたよ
example.english: My wife got mad at me yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: yome no jikka ni ikimasu
examplePolite.ja: 嫁の実家に行きます
examplePolite.english: I'm going to my wife's parents' place.

items.notes: Some find it old-fashioned; tsuma is the neutral word.

blocks.label: Family roles
blocks.rationale: Lets you describe parents and eldest children as roles.
blocks.interference: chichioya and hahaoya describe a role; they are not what you call your parents.

items.use: Father as a role ('a father', 'his father'), not what you call him.

example.ja: 彼、もう父親なんだ
example.english: He's a dad now.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa mou chichioya desu
examplePolite.ja: 彼はもう父親です
examplePolite.english: He's a father now.

items.use: Mother as a role ('a mother', 'her mother'), not what you call her.

example.ja: 母親にそっくりだね
example.english: You look just like your mother.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo wa futari no ko no hahaoya desu
examplePolite.ja: 彼女は二人の子の母親です
examplePolite.english: She's a mother of two.

example.ja: あの二人、親子みたい
example.english: Those two look like parent and child.

examplePolite.romaji: oyako de sanka dekimasu
examplePolite.ja: 親子で参加できます
examplePolite.english: Parents and children can take part together.

items.notes: Oyakodon, chicken and egg on rice, is named after it.

example.ja: 俺、長男だからさ
example.english: I'm the eldest son, you know.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa chounan desu
examplePolite.ja: 私は長男です
examplePolite.english: I'm the eldest son.

items.notes: Often carries family duties, like looking after the parents.

example.ja: あたし、長女なんだ
example.english: I'm the eldest daughter.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa choujo desu
examplePolite.ja: 私は長女です
examplePolite.english: I'm the eldest daughter.

items.notes: The second son and daughter are jinan and jijo.

blocks.label: Grandparents and grandchildren
blocks.rationale: Lets you mention your grandparents and grandkids politely.
blocks.interference: sofu and sobo are your own grandparents in polite talk; at home say ojiichan and obaachan.

items.use: Your own grandchild; someone else's is omagosan.

example.ja: 孫がかわいくてしょうがない
example.english: My grandkids are just too cute.

examplePolite.romaji: mago ga sannin imasu
examplePolite.ja: 孫が三人います
examplePolite.english: I have three grandchildren.

items.use: Your own grandfather in polite talk with outsiders; at home say ojiichan.

example.romaji: sofu ga kyonen nakunatta n da
example.ja: 祖父が去年亡くなったんだ
example.english: My grandfather passed away last year.

examplePolite.romaji: sofu wa moto kyoushi desu
examplePolite.ja: 祖父は元教師です
examplePolite.english: My grandfather is a retired teacher.

items.use: Your own grandmother in polite talk with outsiders; at home say obaachan.

example.romaji: sobo no ie, inaka ni aru n da
example.ja: 祖母の家、田舎にあるんだ
example.english: My grandmother's house is in the countryside.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa sobo ni sodateraremashita
examplePolite.ja: 私は祖母に育てられました
examplePolite.english: I was raised by my grandmother.

blocks.label: Rough home words
blocks.rationale: Lets you understand the homely or blunt words people use for family.
blocks.interference: oyaji and ofukuro are men's words for their own parents; oyaji also means any middle-aged man.

items.use: Men's casual word for their own father; also any middle-aged man, or the owner of a small shop.

example.ja: 昨日親父とケンカした
example.english: I had a fight with my old man yesterday.

items.use: Homely, old-fashioned way to call your mother; also in rough men's talk.

example.ja: 母ちゃん、お腹すいたよ
example.english: Ma, I'm hungry.

items.notes: okaasan is the standard word; to outsiders, your own mother is haha.

items.use: Men's casual word for their own mother when talking to others.

example.romaji: ofukuro no ryouri ga ichiban da yo
example.ja: おふくろの料理が一番だよ
example.english: Nothing beats my mum's cooking.

items.notes: Ofukuro no aji means home cooking like Mum makes.

items.use: Homely, old-fashioned way to call your father.

example.ja: 父ちゃん、早く帰ってきてね
example.english: Come home early, Dad.

items.notes: otousan is the standard word; to outsiders, your own father is chichi.

items.use: Blunt word for an old man or your own grandpa; can sound rude.

example.ja: あのじいさん、また怒ってるよ
example.english: That old guy's angry again.

blocks.label: Hair, skin and nails
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about grooming and how skin looks.
blocks.interference: kami no ke and kami are the same hair; ke alone is body hair.

items.use: Same hair as kami but more concrete, often single hairs or hair that has fallen out.

example.romaji: suupu ni kami no ke haitteru
example.ja: スープに髪の毛入ってる
example.english: There's a hair in the soup.

examplePolite.romaji: suupu ni kami no ke ga haitte imasu
examplePolite.ja: スープに髪の毛が入っています
examplePolite.english: There's a hair in the soup.

items.use: Mostly about how skin looks or feels.

example.ja: 肌きれいだね
example.english: Your skin is so nice.

examplePolite.romaji: hada ga kirei desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 肌がきれいですね
examplePolite.english: Your skin is lovely.

items.notes: The doctor's word for skin is hifu.

example.ja: 爪伸びてきた、切らなきゃ
example.english: My nails have grown, I need to cut them.

examplePolite.romaji: tsume ga nobita node kirimasu
examplePolite.ja: 爪が伸びたので切ります
examplePolite.english: My nails have grown, so I'll cut them.

items.notes: Nail clippers are tsumekiri.

blocks.label: Left, right, both
blocks.rationale: Lets you say which hand, or the whole body.
blocks.interference: None.

example.ja: 昨日右手をけがした
example.english: I hurt my right hand yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou migite o kega shimashita
examplePolite.ja: 昨日右手をけがしました
examplePolite.english: I hurt my right hand yesterday.

items.notes: Migite also means on the right-hand side, as in directions.

example.ja: 左手で箸使える？
example.english: Can you use chopsticks with your left hand?

examplePolite.romaji: hidarite de hashi o tsukaemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 左手で箸を使えますか？
examplePolite.english: Can you use chopsticks with your left hand?

items.notes: Hidarite also means on the left-hand side, as in directions.

example.ja: 重いから両手で持って
example.english: It's heavy, hold it with both hands.

examplePolite.romaji: omoi node ryoute de motte kudasai
examplePolite.ja: 重いので両手で持ってください
examplePolite.english: It's heavy, so please hold it with both hands.

example.romaji: kinou no jimu de zenshin kinnikutsuu
example.ja: 昨日のジムで全身筋肉痛
example.english: I'm sore all over from yesterday's gym session.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou no jimu de zenshin ga itai desu
examplePolite.ja: 昨日のジムで全身が痛いです
examplePolite.english: My whole body aches from yesterday's gym session.

blocks.label: Front and far side
blocks.rationale: Say something is right in front, across, at the back, just before, or face-on.
blocks.interference: temae (this side) vs mukou (the far side); oku (deep inside) vs ushiro (behind).

items.use: The far side of something: kawa no mukou = across the river.

example.romaji: ano biru no mukou ni kouen ga aru yo.
example.ja: あのビルの向こうに公園があるよ。
example.english: There's a park on the other side of that building.

examplePolite.romaji: ano biru no mukou ni kouen ga arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: あのビルの向こうに公園があります。
examplePolite.english: There's a park on the other side of that building.

items.notes: Also 'they, the other party', or 'abroad': mukou de = over there.

items.use: Right in front, very close: eki no me no mae = right across from the station.

example.romaji: hoteru wa eki no me no mae da yo.
example.ja: ホテルは駅の目の前だよ。
example.english: The hotel's right in front of the station.

examplePolite.romaji: hoteru wa eki no me no mae desu.
examplePolite.ja: ホテルは駅の目の前です。
examplePolite.english: The hotel is right in front of the station.

items.notes: Also 'coming right up': shiken ga me no mae = the exam is almost here.

items.use: The far end inside a space: mise no oku = the back of the shop.

example.ja: トイレ、奥にあるよ。
example.english: The toilet's at the back.

examplePolite.romaji: toire wa oku ni arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: トイレは奥にあります。
examplePolite.english: The toilet is at the back.

items.notes: ushiro is behind something; oku is deep inside it.

items.use: In directions: eki no temae = just before you reach the station.

example.ja: 駅の手前で降ろして。
example.english: Drop me off just before the station.

examplePolite.romaji: eki no temae de oroshite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 駅の手前で降ろしてください。
examplePolite.english: Please drop me off just before the station.

items.notes: The rough 'temee!' (you!) heard in films comes from it.

items.use: The main face of a building, or straight across from you.

example.ja: 正面の入口から入って。
example.english: Come in through the front entrance.

examplePolite.romaji: shoumen no iriguchi kara haitte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 正面の入口から入ってください。
examplePolite.english: Please come in through the front entrance.

items.notes: mae is just 'in front'; shoumen is face-on.

blocks.label: Middle, sides, all over
blocks.rationale: Talk about the surroundings, one side, the middle, and all over the place.
blocks.interference: mannaka (exact middle) vs naka (inside).

items.english: around; surroundings; the people around you
items.use: mawari no hito = the people around you, a big deal in Japanese social life.

example.romaji: mawari no hito, ki ni shinakute ii yo.
example.ja: 周りの人、気にしなくていいよ。
example.english: Don't worry about the people around you.

examplePolite.romaji: mawari no hito wa ki ni shinakute ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 周りの人は気にしなくていいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You don't need to worry about the people around you.

items.notes: Physical sense too: eki no mawari = around the station.

items.use: Attaches to a place or direction: migigawa (right side), kotchigawa (this side), mukougawa (far side).

example.ja: こっち側の席に座って。
example.english: Sit on this side.

examplePolite.romaji: kochiragawa no seki ni suwatte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: こちら側の席に座ってください。
examplePolite.english: Please sit on this side.

items.notes: Also a side in a dispute: kaisha no gawa = the company's side.

example.romaji: mannaka no seki ga ii na.
example.ja: 真ん中の席がいいな。
example.english: I'd like the middle seat.

examplePolite.romaji: mannaka no seki ga ii desu.
examplePolite.ja: 真ん中の席がいいです。
examplePolite.english: I'd like the middle seat, please.

items.notes: naka is 'inside'; mannaka is the exact middle.

example.ja: 昨日あちこち探したけど、なかった。
example.english: I looked all over yesterday, but it wasn't there.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou achikochi sagashimashita ga, arimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日あちこち探しましたが、ありませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I searched all over yesterday, but it wasn't there.

items.notes: Casually said atchikotchi. karada no achikochi ga itai = I ache all over.

blocks.label: Compass points
blocks.rationale: Use north, south, east and west, mostly for station exits and regions.
blocks.interference: higashi and hidari both start hi-; kita 'north' sounds like kita 'came'.

items.use: Big stations name exits by direction: kitaguchi = north exit.

example.romaji: kita no hou wa mada yuki ga aru yo.
example.ja: 北の方はまだ雪があるよ。
example.english: There's still snow up north.

examplePolite.romaji: kita no hou wa mada yuki ga arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 北の方はまだ雪がありますよ。
examplePolite.english: There's still snow in the north.

items.notes: Same sound as kita 'came'.

items.use: minamiguchi = the south exit of a station.

example.ja: じゃあ、南口で待ってるね。
example.english: OK, I'll wait at the south exit.

examplePolite.romaji: dewa, minamiguchi de matte imasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: では、南口で待っていますね。
examplePolite.english: Then I'll be waiting at the south exit.

items.use: higashiguchi = the east exit of a station.

example.romaji: higashiguchi kara deta hou ga chikai yo.
example.ja: 東口から出た方が近いよ。
example.english: It's quicker if you leave by the east exit.

examplePolite.romaji: higashiguchi kara deta hou ga chikai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 東口から出た方が近いですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's closer if you leave by the east exit.

items.notes: Don't mix up with hidari (left); both start hi-.

items.use: nishiguchi = the west exit of a station; nishi nihon = western Japan.

example.ja: 駅の西口ってどっち？
example.english: Which way's the station's west exit?

examplePolite.romaji: eki no nishiguchi wa dochira desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 駅の西口はどちらですか？
examplePolite.english: Which way is the station's west exit?

blocks.label: Formal and self words
blocks.rationale: Lets you mention someone respectfully, speak for a group, and say yourself.
blocks.interference: jibun jishin stresses the self; plain jibun is the everyday word.

items.use: Respectful ano hito, for customers, elders and bosses.

example.romaji: ano kata ga shachou desu yo
example.ja: あの方が社長ですよ
example.english: That's the company president.

items.notes: Also kono kata and sono kata; the polite 'who' is donata.

items.use: Speeches, business and speaking for a group; stiff or jokey in chat.

example.ja: 我々の勝利だ！
example.english: Victory is ours!

examplePolite.romaji: wareware wa kono keikaku ni hantai desu
examplePolite.ja: 我々はこの計画に反対です
examplePolite.english: We are against this plan.

items.use: Stresses the self: jibun jishin de kimeru means decide for yourself.

example.ja: もっと自分自身を信じて
example.english: Believe in yourself more.

examplePolite.romaji: motto jibun jishin o shinjite kudasai
examplePolite.ja: もっと自分自身を信じてください
examplePolite.english: Please believe in yourself more.

items.notes: Jibun alone is the everyday 'oneself'.

cuts.english: one day; a day (per day); a whole day

cuts.reason: Tokenizer fragment of X-ji han (e.g. sanji han); covered by 半 (han) and 一時 (-ji).
Duplicate of 私たち (same word, written with kanji 達).
Spelling variant of か月; the same -kagetsu counter.
